location.sentence_range: s600 (Design rail 7) vs s326 (rule 4) vs s263 (README registers)

quote: same paper under "supportive" vs neutral framing → identical must-fix list.
issue: The tone-invariance ACCEPTANCE TEST is stated with a third register the tool never defines, and it contradicts the constitution's own statement of the identical test. Design v1 rail 7 says the test is "supportive" vs "neutral" framing. But the tool defines exactly two registers — README: "Register: `supportive` (default) · `brutal` (delivery tone only — severity never changes)." — and the binding constitution states the SAME acceptance test as "supportive" vs "brutal" (grounding rule 4: "the *same* manuscript reviewed under 'supportive' vs. 'brutal' framing must return an identical must-fix list"). So rail 7 (a) invokes a 'neutral' register that exists nowhere else and is not selectable, and (b) names a different register pair than the constitution for what is explicitly called the build's pass/fail acceptance test. The precedence rule (C-030, 'this file wins') resolves it in favor of the constitution's 'brutal' wording — but only for prompts-vs-constitution; a builder reading Design v1 (a design doc, not a prompt) has no cue to apply it, and could wire the harness to a non-existent 'neutral' mode.
why_it_matters: Tone-invariance is a headline guarantee (README: 'the same paper reviewed "supportively" or "brutally" returns the same must-fix list'). The one mechanical check that is supposed to enforce that guarantee is specified inconsistently and against an undefined register, so 'the build passes the acceptance test' has no single well-defined meaning. A self-audit that ships this leaves its central trust claim un-pinned.
proposed_fix: In Design v1 rail 7, change 'supportive" vs neutral framing' to 'supportive" vs "brutal" framing' so the acceptance test matches grounding rule 4 and the two defined registers. (If a distinct internal 'neutral' baseline is genuinely intended, define it as a register in README/SKILL and in grounding rule 4 so all three agree.)
risk_of_fix: Low. If the author actually intends three registers, a blind one-word edit would mask that design gap rather than surface it — hence the parenthetical alternative; the author should confirm only two registers exist.

location.section: SKILL.md (entry point & claims) Files block vs DESIGN v1 §5 Repo layout

issue: Two normative file-layout statements give directly conflicting prompt-numbering ranges for the same directory. SKILL.md says Act I prompts are '00..07' and Act II prompts are 'phase2/10..16'. Design v1 §5 says Act I prompts are '00_scout_roster … 09_chair_synthesis' and Act II prompts are 'phase2/{10_implementer…13_repro_package}'. Act I therefore ends at 07 in one place and 09 in another; Act II spans 10–16 in one place and 10–13 in the other. For a design document being prepped for first public release, the canonical file manifest disagreeing with itself is a concrete spec-conformance defect.
proposed_fix: Pick one numbering and make both blocks identical — e.g. align SKILL.md to '00..09 (Act I) + phase2/10..13 (Act II)' to match Design v1 §5 and the '09_chair_synthesis' references in §5/§6; or update Design v1 if the true count differs. State the prompt count once and reference it.

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (precedence rule, C-030) — scope gap relative to SKILL.md / README / DESIGN v1

issue: The document set's only precedence / tie-breaker rule is scoped to prompts versus the constitution: 'Where a later prompt seems to conflict with this file, this file wins' (C-030). But the substantive conflicts in this manuscript (prompt-numbering range, schemas/ contents and spine filename, examples/ directory name, the acceptance-test register) are SKILL.md-vs-Design-v1 and README-vs-Design-v1 — documentation-vs-documentation, neither of which is 'a later prompt' and neither of which is 'this file'. The only 'supersedes' language present (Design v1 header) supersedes an earlier *pilot verdict*, not SKILL.md or README. So the manuscript provides NO rule for which document is authoritative when SKILL.md, README, and Design v1 disagree — and they demonstrably do. The silence is what lets the contradictions in S01-F1..F4 stand unresolved.
why_it_matters: A multi-file spec that contradicts itself is recoverable IF it declares a source of truth; this one does not, so a reader/implementer has no principled way to resolve the discrepancies, and the elegant 'this file wins' rule creates a false impression that precedence is handled when it only covers the prompt layer. Declaring authority is a cheap, high-leverage fix that dissolves several findings at once.
proposed_fix: Add a one-line authority statement to the grounding rules (or SKILL.md) of the form 'For file layout, schema names, prompt numbering, and tier/register definitions, SKILL.md is canonical; Design v1 is design rationale and yields to SKILL.md where they differ' — then reconcile S01-F1..F4 to that source of truth.
risk_of_fix: Low-to-moderate: naming SKILL.md canonical is only safe if SKILL.md is then actually corrected to the intended values (e.g. the '00..07' range and the 5-vs-4 schema list) — otherwise the authority rule would bless the wrong numbers. Author should confirm which document holds the intended truth before designating it.

location.section: helpers/quote_gate.py (helper, as concatenated) + prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution)

quote:
An LLM verifier shares the
    hallucination it is checking, so this gate is a **script**, fail-closed.
issue: The gate is claimed to be 'fail-closed', but its batch path fails OPEN for a malformed finding. In cmd_batch, the exempt branch only triggers when finding_type=='absence-silence' AND the quote normalizes to empty; otherwise control falls to check(quote, source), and check() itself returns (True, 'exempt-absence') for ANY quote that normalizes to empty (including a whitespace-only quote). I verified this directly against the actual helper: a finding typed 'statistical' with quote '   ' yields matched=True, match_level='exempt-absence', and cmd_batch assigns it severity_hint='keep' — i.e. an empty/whitespace quote on a NON-absence finding is reported as a passing, exempt match rather than failing closed. A fabricated or malformed finding that carries no real anchoring quote is therefore waved through with the same verdict as a legitimate absence-silence finding, defeating the one deterministic line of defense the design leans on. (Reachability caveat: this requires an upstream finding to reach the gate with an empty/whitespace quote and a non-absence type; the gate is nonetheless asserted to be fail-closed unconditionally, so the script not failing closed is a defect on the design's own terms.)
why_it_matters: C-013 and C-038 make the deterministic, fail-closed quote-gate the load-bearing reason a same-model fleet can be trusted ('not an LLM'; 'fail-closed'). If the script returns a passing 'exempt-absence' verdict for an empty quote on a non-absence finding, the guarantee that every non-absence finding is anchored by a verbatim quote does not actually hold in code.
proposed_fix: In check(), only return the exempt-absence short-circuit when the CALLER declares the finding is absence-typed; otherwise an empty normalized quote must return (False, 'none'). Concretely, move the empty-quote exemption entirely into cmd_batch's is_absence branch and have check() treat nq=='' as a non-match (fail-closed). Add a unit test asserting that a non-absence finding with an empty/whitespace quote returns matched=False.
risk_of_fix: If any non-absence finding type legitimately ships an intentionally empty quote (none is documented), this would start failing it — which is the intended fail-closed behavior, but callers relying on the current lenient return would need updating. The single-check CLI (cmd_check) shares check(), so an empty --quote would flip from matched=True to matched=False; confirm no workflow depends on the old behavior.

location.section: helpers/verification_panel.md (the multi-angle gate) — Principles + Delivery rule (Act I)

quote: A finding that cannot survive a determined defense should not ship.
issue: The steelman-charity angle is given veto power over true findings, and at the default tier nothing redundant or deterministic checks it. The table entry is 'steelman-charity ... strong defense ⇒ reject', and the Act-I delivery rule says a finding is delivered iff '... it is not killed by a strong steelman defense ...'. Whether a defense is 'strong' is an LLM judgment, not code. At 'thorough' the panel runs only '≥1 verifier on each soft angle', so a SINGLE charity verifier — the one angle explicitly instructed to argue FOR the paper — can unilaterally suppress a genuinely fatal finding, which is then routed to rejected_suggestions and never delivered to the author. The design correctly worries (C-038) that an LLM verifier shares the hallucination it checks, yet here an LLM is the sole gatekeeper deciding whether real criticism dies.
why_it_matters: This is squarely the failure mode my jurisdiction names: the steelman/charity angle CAN veto true findings. A suppressed High finding never reaches the user, so the tool's central promise (a 300-600-agent run will not launder a fatal flaw into a green light, C-012) is defeated not by missing the flaw but by a single charity-verifier killing it after it was found.
proposed_fix: Make steelman-charity non-vetoing on its own: a 'strong defense' should DOWNGRADE-with-record or route the finding to the author with the defense attached, not silently reject it, mirroring how a failed quote-locator forces needs-author-confirmation rather than deletion. If charity must be able to reject, require ≥2 independent charity verifiers to concur even at 'thorough', and never let charity reject a finding the author has not seen. Persist every charity-rejected High/Med finding visibly (not only in rejected_suggestions) so the author can override.
risk_of_fix: Weakening charity's veto raises the false-positive rate the design is trying to suppress — trivially-defended findings could resurface and bloat the must-fix list. Mitigate by keeping decision-relevance/severity-calibration as demote (not delete) paths and by surfacing charity-defended items in an appendix rather than the headline ledger.

location.section: helpers/verification_panel.md (the multi-angle gate) — Principles ('Blind', 'One angle per verifier')

issue: The design uses the shared-hallucination argument to justify a CODE quote-gate ('An LLM verifier shares the hallucination it is checking, so this gate is a script') but never applies the same argument to the six LLM verification angles (logical-validity, factual-literature, severity-calibration, decision-relevance, steelman-charity, fix-safety), which are all the same base model. The only decorrelation offered for the panel is blindness ('a verifier that can see another's verdict is contaminated') and 'one angle per verifier'. Blindness removes the verdict-leakage correlation channel but does nothing about the dominant correlation source the document itself identifies elsewhere: same-model seats are 'N correlated draws' sharing a common prior. A shared blind spot — a method the base model misjudges, a citation it consistently misremembers, a fallacy it does not register — will be missed by every angle simultaneously, and no amount of angle-diversity or blindness catches an error all instances share. The manuscript is silent on why the very argument that forced the quote-gate into code does not also undercut the LLM panel, and offers no empirical decorrelation evidence (no inter-verifier disagreement rate, no planted-error catch rate per angle) for the panel as it does promise for the seats (the C-068 ablation targets recall/FPR of findings, not verifier independence).
why_it_matters: The panel (grounding rule 8; C-043, C-044) is the gate that lets the tool be 'monumental without being a confident-nonsense generator'. If its independence is only verdict-blindness on a single shared model, then for any error the base model reliably makes, the panel provides no protection — the same structural weakness the design explicitly rejects for quote-checking. This is the load-bearing soundness question for the whole verification mechanism and it is unaddressed.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit treatment of same-model verifier correlation: (a) state plainly that the LLM angles share a common prior and therefore cannot catch errors the base model reliably makes, scoping the panel's guarantee accordingly; (b) route the highest-stakes angles to a deterministic check wherever possible (extend the code-backed set), and where not possible, use a different model or the consent-gated external dissent leg for at least one angle; (c) report an empirical inter-verifier decorrelation diagnostic (per-angle catch rate on planted errors, cross-verifier disagreement rate) alongside the seat-level recall/FPR validation, so the independence claim is measured, not asserted.
risk_of_fix: Adding a non-Claude angle conflicts with the 'Claude-only' identity (C-009) and the privacy posture for confidential manuscripts; the fix must keep that leg optional, abstracted, and consent-gated. Scoping the guarantee honestly may read as weakening the headline, but it is the accurate claim.

location.section: helpers/verification_panel.md (the multi-angle gate) — verifier-count threshold

quote: Run **≥3 verifiers on the hard-gate angles and ≥1 on each soft angle** at `thorough`
issue: The hard-gate verifier-count threshold is ambiguous in a way that changes the safety floor. 'Run ≥3 verifiers on the hard-gate angles' does not specify whether that is ≥3 PER hard-gate angle or ≥3 TOTAL distributed across the (three Act-I) hard-gate angles. The natural reading — 3 verifiers spread over the 3 hard-gate angles (quote-locator, logical-validity, fix-safety) — yields exactly ONE verifier per hard gate, so a single LLM verdict would decide logical-validity, which the table marks 'fail ⇒ reject'. That is a hard REJECT gate decided by one model, with no majority and no redundancy, at the default tier most users will run. The 'exhaustive/monumental' line is explicit ('2 independent verifiers per angle (majority within an angle)'); the 'thorough' line is not, and the most likely reading leaves the default tier's hard gates single-verifier.
why_it_matters: Whether a hard reject gate is single- or multi-verifier at the default tier is load-bearing for both false negatives (a real finding wrongly rejected by one logical-validity verifier) and the tool's claim of redundancy. An ambiguous threshold that resolves to single-verifier hard gates undercuts 'several independent subagents' (C-043) at the tier most runs use.
proposed_fix: State the count per angle explicitly, e.g. 'at thorough: ≥1 verifier per soft angle and ≥2 (majority) per hard-gate angle that is LLM-decided; the code-backed quote-locator needs only 1 run since it is deterministic.' This also resolves the oddity of demanding 3 verifiers for the quote-locator angle, which is a deterministic script where one run suffices.
risk_of_fix: Raising the per-angle floor at thorough increases agent count and runtime for the default tier; if the intended design really was 3-total, the author should confirm which they meant before the wording is pinned, since it changes the cost model.

location.section: helpers/quote_gate.py (helper, as concatenated) — dehyphenate fallback

issue: The dehyphenate fallback can manufacture a FALSE positive match. dehyphenate() strips every '-' that is followed by whitespace and is applied to BOTH the quote and the source, so a quote string that never appears verbatim can match. I verified against the actual helper: with source 'the cost- benefit and the risk- reward tradeoff' (PDF-style line-break hyphens), the candidate quote 'costbenefit and the riskreward' — which appears nowhere as written — returns matched=True, match_level='dehyphenated'. Separately, normalize() collapses ALL whitespace including newlines, so a quote that stitches text across a column/table-cell break (e.g. 'value Column2' against 'value\nColumn2') also matches as 'normalized'. Both are narrow and require an unusual quote, and the dehyphenation is a deliberate accommodation for PDF line-break hyphenation, so this is a low-severity edge rather than the empty-quote defect in S02-F1.
why_it_matters: The gate is presented as a 1:1 substring check that prevents fabricated quotes (C-013, C-018). A normalization that can return a verbatim-true verdict for a string the author never wrote slightly widens the surface for a fabricated or stitched quote to pass; it should be acknowledged and bounded even though it is hard to trigger accidentally.
proposed_fix: Only apply the dehyphenation fallback at positions that were genuinely line-break hyphens (e.g. require the hyphen to be immediately followed by a newline in the ORIGINAL source before collapsing, rather than any '-' + whitespace after normalization). Optionally record match_level='dehyphenated' as a weaker tier that triggers a human spot-check. Document that the gate guarantees a normalized substring match, not a glyph-exact one.
risk_of_fix: Tightening dehyphenation could reintroduce false NEGATIVES for genuinely hyphenated PDF line breaks (the case the fallback exists to handle), pushing legitimate quotes to needs-author-confirmation. The change should be tested against real PDF-extracted hyphenated quotes before adoption.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims), §2.4 'The deliverable bundle (why it beats any conference)'

quote: The "better than a conference" feeling = a world authority on *every* sub-part
issue: The headline superiority claim ('better than any conference', tier table line 98) is, by the design's OWN definition, a 'feeling' manufactured by asserting that simulated LLM subagents are 'a world authority on *every* sub-part'. No mechanism in the design substantiates either the comparison to a real conference or the 'world authority' premise. Worse, the premise is contradicted by the document's own load-bearing rationale for the deterministic quote gate: 'An LLM verifier shares the hallucination it is checking' (verification_panel.md section, and grounding rule 10). A fleet whose members are explicitly NOT trusted to verify their own quotes cannot simultaneously be marketed as a panel of world authorities whose collective judgment beats a conference. The contribution claim is therefore not what the design can deliver.
why_it_matters: This is the central marketing claim of the artifact and it is sized far beyond what the mechanism supports. A referee evaluating the contribution would reject the framing on this point alone: the design asks the reader to treat a 'feeling' produced by same-model subagents as equivalent-or-superior to a panel of actual human experts, while elsewhere conceding those same subagents cannot be trusted to verify a substring. Tone-invariant: this is a validity/contribution problem, not a wording nicety.
proposed_fix: Replace the 'better than any conference' / 'world authority on every sub-part' framing with a defensible, falsifiable claim about what the tool actually provides (e.g., 'a large, decorrelated, quote-grounded, multi-angle-verified critique fleet'), and explicitly disclaim simulated-authority equivalence to human experts. Reserve any comparative-superiority language until the §6.8 validation track has produced a result.
risk_of_fix: Softening the brand language could read as under-selling a genuinely novel scale advantage; the fix must preserve the real differentiators (rival-objective decorrelation, code quote-gate, coverage proof) while dropping only the unsupported superlatives.

location.section: SKILL.md (entry point & claims), description block

quote:
produces an
  impeccable revised paper plus a full replication package
issue: 'Impeccable' is an absolute, flawless-output guarantee. No mechanism in the design can deliver it, and it directly contradicts two of the tool's own non-negotiable rules: grounding rule 15 ('Honest labeling' — a run may be degraded and must say so) and grounding rule 14 ('The author is the author' — substantive judgments are only proposed, ratified by the human). A tool that can emit a self-declared degraded run, and that explicitly does NOT certify scientific correctness (only that edits are quote/number-grounded and author-approved), cannot promise an 'impeccable' paper. The same absolute appears as a section title (§3): 'Act II — ATELIER (opt-in → impeccable paper + replication package)'.
why_it_matters: The promised contribution (an 'impeccable' output) is strictly stronger than what the design's own rails permit, so the contribution claim is not supported by the evidence/design. Promising flawlessness while the constitution simultaneously says runs can be degraded is an internal contradiction a referee would flag as an overclaim that undermines the document's credibility.
proposed_fix: Replace 'impeccable' (both in the SKILL.md description and the §3 heading) with an accurate, bounded descriptor such as 'a verified, tracked-change revised paper' or 'a much-improved, fully audit-trailed paper', consistent with the 'much-improved' wording already used at §0 line 511.
risk_of_fix: Low risk; the change is a deflation toward language the document already uses elsewhere ('much-improved'). Care only that the replacement not over-deflate into implying the output is unverified.

location.section: Whole document (esp. README §'Why you can trust a 300-agent run', SKILL.md tier table, DESIGN v1 §6.8)

issue: The document makes multiple comparative-superiority and quality claims — 'better than any conference' (line 98), 'the largest, most rigorous critique Claude can produce' (line 165), 'why you can trust a 300-agent run', 'the moat' (line 641) — but contains NO completed evidence for any of them. The only validation is described as future, optional, and non-blocking: 'Validation track (parallel, non-blocking): 4-arm ablation ... score recall AND false-positive rate; use it to *tune the default fan-out* and headline the README with a real number — not as a gate.' (line 634). The examples/ directory is labeled 'self-audit/ (the tool run on itself)' and 'optimal-inflation-pilot/ (first worked example)' — i.e., no recall/false-positive numbers exist yet. Thus every superiority claim is currently unfalsified and unsupported; the load-bearing evidence is admitted-absent.
why_it_matters: For an artifact whose entire value proposition is rigor and superiority over alternatives, shipping the comparative claims BEFORE the benchmark that would substantiate them is exactly the 'marketing-vs-substance' gap this seat exists to catch. A referee would treat the central claims as unestablished until the validation track reports. This is the most severe item because it is the missing load-bearing analysis behind the headline contribution.
proposed_fix: Either (a) gate all comparative-superiority language behind the completed validation track (state plainly, per grounding rule 15, that no recall/false-positive numbers exist yet and the superiority claims are aspirational), or (b) run the §6.8 ablation on the named pilots and replace the slogans with the measured numbers. Until then, demote 'better than any conference' and 'most rigorous critique Claude can produce' to clearly-labeled design goals.
risk_of_fix: If the disclaimer is added without also keeping the genuine, already-true claims (quote-gating, coverage proof, rival-objective decorrelation), the document could under-represent real, deliverable features. The fix must separate 'true today' from 'goal pending validation', not blanket-hedge everything.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims), §8 'Relationship to mad-research'

quote: is the moat — nothing in the lineage does it
issue: Two distinct claims about cited sibling works are asserted as fact without a staged source: (1) the factual claim that mad-research 'explicitly does **not** run code' (line 641; mirrored in the README comparison table line 272 'Code | does **not** run it') and that 'nothing in the lineage does it', and (2) the framing claim that running the author's code 'is the moat'. Per grounding rules 1 and 11, claims about cited works must be checked against the fetched original, not memory; STAGED_SOURCES_DIR is '(none)', so neither mad-research nor research-audit-duel-protocol was fetched, and the 'does not run code' / 'nothing in the lineage does it' assertions are unverified. Separately, 'moat' is a durable-competitive-advantage claim that a design document cannot establish for itself — it overclaims defensibility from a single un-validated feature.
why_it_matters: The differentiation from mad-research is the paper's core positioning, and it rests on an unverified factual assertion about a cited tool plus an unsupported 'moat' framing. If mad-research can in fact run code (or a lineage tool does), the central contribution claim collapses; even if it cannot, asserting it without grounding violates the document's own constitution. This is the related-work-honesty failure this seat owns.
proposed_fix: Ground the comparison: cite the specific mad-research line/section that states it does not run code (or correct the claim if it can), and drop or heavily qualify 'moat' to a defensible phrasing such as 'the primary capability that distinguishes it from mad-research in this lineage'. Mark the inter-tool comparison needs-author-confirmation until the sibling repos are fetched and quoted.
risk_of_fix: If mad-research's behavior is mis-stated in the correction, a new related-work error is introduced; the fix must quote the sibling repo verbatim rather than restate from memory. Removing 'moat' risks weakening the positioning, so pair it with the grounded differentiator.

location.section: README.md (public claims), §'Relationship to mad-research' comparison table

quote: | Code | does **not** run it | **re-runs it** and ships the replication package |
issue: The comparison table contrasts a *shipped* mad-research against paper-workshop capabilities that the document itself marks as unbuilt/aspirational. The 'Code | re-runs it' and 'Output | memo + implemented paper + replication package' rows describe Act II, which the roadmap lists as future work 'built against a pilot with real data/code' (line 633) and whose validation is 'parallel, non-blocking' (line 634); the only example is the 'first worked example' (line 622) / self-audit. Presenting future Act II capability as a present-tense column entry, side-by-side with a real competitor's present capability, is an asymmetric, self-favorable comparison — the reader cannot tell that one side of the table is not yet demonstrated.
why_it_matters: A comparison table is read as a statement of current fact. Sizing paper-workshop's not-yet-demonstrated Act II against mad-research's existing behavior inflates the contribution relative to the lineage. A referee would require that aspirational rows be labeled as design targets, not delivered features.
proposed_fix: Annotate the table to distinguish delivered vs. planned capabilities (e.g., mark Act II rows 'design target; pilot pending'), or restrict the table to Act I (which is described as shippable, line 632) and describe Act II separately with its build status stated honestly per grounding rule 15.
risk_of_fix: Labeling Act II as planned could blunt the headline differentiator; mitigate by keeping the differentiator prominent while being explicit that it is not yet validated, so the table is honest without burying the genuine novelty.

location.section: README.md (public claims), opening positioning paragraph

quote:
It is built for power users who want the largest, most rigorous critique Claude can
produce
issue: 'The largest, most rigorous critique Claude can produce' is an unfalsifiable superlative asserted with no comparison, baseline, or definition of 'rigorous'. location.section: README.md (public claims), Act II bullet list

quote: and clean-room-replicates it to prove it reproduces

location.section: SKILL.md (entry point & claims) / README.md / helpers/verification_panel.md (the multi-angle gate)

issue: The headline trust-at-scale claim is that the rails 'keep a 300-600-agent run from laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light' (s47). But that failure mode is a correlated FALSE NEGATIVE: a real fatal flaw that no producing seat raises. The manuscript provides no mechanism against it, and never discusses it. Every verification angle except the deterministic quote-gate (logical-validity, factual-literature, severity-calibration, decision-relevance, steelman-charity, fix-safety) is a same-model Claude subagent. The paper itself states the governing principle that defeats them: 'An LLM verifier shares the hallucination it is checking, so this gate is a script, fail-closed' (s309) — the reason the QUOTE gate is code. That reasoning applies identically to the six non-code angles: if the homogeneous producing fleet shares a blind spot (a wrong belief, a missed assumption), the homogeneous verifier fleet shares it too, so nothing fires. The verification panel only AUDITS candidate outputs ('The panel audits candidate outputs — findings and edits'); it cannot surface a flaw that was never proposed. The completeness audit certifies 'covered == total' (s155) — attention, not correctness; a fully-covered, fully-verified ledger can still miss the one fatal flaw. The single decorrelating mechanism against shared blind spots — the external dissent leg asking 'what did all Claude seats miss?' (s602) — is off by default and skippable. A search of the manuscript finds 'false negative', 'blind spot', and 'correlated error' nowhere; 'recall' appears only as a planned non-blocking validation metric (s647), never as a runtime property. The design is demonstrably engineered against false POSITIVES (the stopping rule, finding-killer, and steelman all fight manufactured/over-stated findings) and is near-silent on the false NEGATIVE that its own central promise is about.
why_it_matters: This is the fatal flaw in my jurisdiction: a 300-600-agent run that misses a real flaw does not merely fail quietly — it ships a completeness certificate, a multi-angle-verified ledger, and a 'world authority on every sub-part' framing, which together manufacture exactly the 'confident green light laundering a fatal flaw' the tool claims to prevent, now with institutional authority behind it. An author or downstream reader will rationally lower their own scrutiny. Because the apparatus has no decorrelated check on shared-model error by default, the strongest scaling claim (C-012, C-051) is unsupported precisely where it matters most.
proposed_fix: Stop claiming the rails prevent laundering a fatal flaw, OR make a decorrelating false-negative check load-bearing rather than optional: (a) make the external (cross-model) dissent leg ON by default for any run that emits a 'competitive'/clean verdict, and explicitly label any run without it as 'single-model, false-negatives not independently checked'; (b) add a standing 'adversarial seeded-flaw canary' — inject known flaws/certified-clean passages each run and report the live miss-rate, so each run shows its own false-negative exposure instead of asserting trust; (c) reframe the certificate as 'coverage + false-positive-controlled', explicitly NOT a false-negative guarantee.
risk_of_fix: Turning the external leg on by default sends abstracted findings to a non-Claude provider, which raises the consent/no-train surface the manuscript currently keeps strictly opt-in (s602, safety_notes); it must stay abstracted-findings-only and consent-gated. A seeded-canary adds runtime and could itself be gamed if seats learn the canary distribution. Neither fix can fully eliminate shared-model blind spots — they bound, not erase, the risk, and the honest reframing (option c) weakens the marketing claim the document leans on.

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution)

quote: is the only thing that makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws.
issue: The load-bearing inference under the whole trust-at-scale argument is invalid as stated. Commit-and-reveal isolation prevents seats from COPYING one another (no cross-talk); it does not change the marginal distribution each seat is sampled from. N isolated draws from one model with shared weights and shared training are still N draws from the same error-prone distribution — independence in the no-cross-talk sense does not deliver decorrelation in the errors-not-shared sense, and only the latter protects against the 'confident green light' failure (S04-F1). The sentence asserts isolation is 'the only thing that makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws', but isolation by itself yields i.i.d. draws, not decorrelated ones: a systematic blind spot is present in every draw regardless of isolation. What actually buys decorrelation is heterogeneity of the generating process (rival objective functions across seats, and the cross-MODEL dissent leg), not isolation per se — yet the document credits isolation with the decorrelation property and then makes the optional cross-model leg the one thing that could supply it.
why_it_matters: If 'independent' is silently equated with 'decorrelated', the entire claim that a large same-model fleet is more trustworthy than a small one collapses at the point that matters for failure-at-scale: more isolated same-model agents do not reduce a shared false-negative rate, they just resample it. This is the mechanism behind S04-F1 and directly undercuts C-012/C-033/C-051 (the trust-because-of-scale story). The fix is conceptual, not cosmetic.
proposed_fix: Distinguish the two notions explicitly in the text: state that commit-and-reveal isolation removes cross-talk/anchoring (a real but limited gain) but does NOT decorrelate model-intrinsic errors, and that protection against shared blind spots comes only from heterogeneity (rival objective functions, and especially the cross-model dissent leg). Soften 'the only thing that makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws' to 'removes one source of correlation (cross-talk); it does not by itself decorrelate errors the base model shares'.
risk_of_fix: This is partly the decorrelation-mechanism territory owned by other seats (S09/S10); the wording change must stay scoped to the at-scale trust consequence and not redesign the mechanism. The honest restatement weakens a sentence the document uses to justify going big, so authors may resist; it should be framed as making the claim defensible rather than retracting it.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — Act II baseline-reproduction gate (s548) and clean-room replication (s601)

issue: Both gates that anchor the entire Act-II provenance guarantee are binary with an UNDEFINED match criterion. The baseline gate is 'Run the author's master script unchanged; diff current headline numbers vs fresh outputs. Match -> baseline_reproduced: true, proceed. Mismatch -> stop and report' (s548), and clean-room replication is 'non-reproducing package can't be marked final' (s601). Nowhere in the manuscript is 'match' / 'reproducing' defined: no floating-point tolerance, no handling of stochastic seeds at the baseline-diff step (seeds are mentioned only for REGENERATION at s585, not for the baseline diff), and no allowance for cross-platform / library-version numeric drift — relevant because runs here are on Windows. A binary gate with an unspecified threshold fails both ways: set it strict (exact/hash match) and essentially every real empirical package 'fails baseline' or 'fails to reproduce' on bitwise differences, so Act II — the stated moat (s660) — never fires; set it loose and a genuinely broken pipeline passes, after which the design will 'improve' numbers on top of it, the exact thing C-061 forbids. The baseline log is called 'the anchor for every later the-number-still-matches check' (phase2_sandbox), so this ambiguity propagates into every downstream provenance assertion. The manuscript also scopes the baseline diff to 'a handful of headline numbers', leaving non-headline numbers unguarded.
why_it_matters: The Execution-Provenance Wall and the 'reproducing replication package' deliverable (C-023, C-024, C-025, C-061, C-065) are only as trustworthy as the pass/fail rule that admits them. An undefined reproduction threshold means the headline integrity guarantees are not operationally testable: the tool cannot, as written, decide reproducibly whether a baseline reproduced, so 'baseline_reproduced: true' and 'package marked final' are judgment calls (made by a Claude subagent, the Replication-Verifier) rather than the deterministic gates the document presents them as. That converts the strongest selling point into theater at the boundary cases that dominate real empirical work.
proposed_fix: Define the match/reproduction criterion in the manuscript: per-quantity relative tolerance (e.g. agree to the precision the paper reports the number to), an explicit seed-fixing-and-recording step BEFORE the baseline diff, an environment-capture requirement, and a documented figure-comparison rule (compare the data behind the figure or a perceptual/structural tolerance, not the PNG hash). State separately the rule for legitimately stochastic vs deterministic outputs, and require the chosen tolerance to be logged with each baseline_reproduced / final decision.
risk_of_fix: Any fixed tolerance is itself a research-integrity lever: too loose silently launders a broken pipeline (the failure C-061 names), too tight blocks legitimate packages and kills the moat. The threshold is partly the author's scientific call (acceptable precision differs by field), so the fix should specify the MACHINERY (per-number tolerance, seed capture, logged decision) and surface the threshold for author sign-off rather than hard-coding one number.

location.section: SKILL.md (entry point & claims) — Safety defaults (s94); cf. README/DESIGN moat claim (s660)

quote: Code re-runs (Act II) execute in a sandbox, **network-off by default**.
issue: The safe default structurally collides with the stated moat. Act II's differentiator is 'running the author's .do/.R/.py and handing back a corrected, reproducing manuscript ... the moat — nothing in the lineage does it' (s660), and the README sells 'Re-runs your actual code'. But real replication packages routinely REQUIRE the network at run time — installing pinned packages from CRAN/PyPI/conda, pulling versioned data or APIs, fetching containers. With 'network-off by default' plus 'Raw data is read-only', a large fraction of realistic packages cannot stand up their environment or fetch their inputs, so the baseline-reproduction gate (S04-F3) fails not because the science is broken but because the sandbox starved it — and the tool's own honest-labeling rule (C-042) then reports 'baseline did not reproduce', degrading the moat exactly on the inputs it most needs to handle. The manuscript never mentions network-dependent packages, offline mirroring/vendoring, or a pre-fetch step. Separately, 'by default' implies the network can be enabled, at which point the tool executes arbitrary untrusted manuscript code with network access — a far larger exfiltration surface than the single, heavily consent-gated external dissent leg the safety section spends most of its words on — yet the manuscript gives this larger surface only the four words 'network-off by default' with no lock, no allowlist, and no per-package review gate.
why_it_matters: The headline Act-II value proposition is the part of the tool with no precedent in the lineage; if it silently degrades to 'edit-spec only' / 'author-decision checklist' whenever a package needs the network (i.e., much of modern empirical work), the moat is narrower than claimed and the document overstates how often Act II actually delivers a reproducing package. The under-specified security default is a second, independent robustness exposure: the dissent leg is fenced with consent and no-train requirements while the much riskier act — running unvetted author code, possibly with the network on — is left to a one-line default.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit dependency-resolution step to Act II: vendor/mirror dependencies and pre-fetch declared data into the read-only input under logged consent BEFORE going network-off, so the actual analysis still runs with no live network; document this as the path for network-dependent packages and label runs where it was not possible as honestly-degraded. For the security default, state that enabling the network requires explicit per-run consent, an egress allowlist, and that author code is always treated as untrusted (no broad permissions), mirroring the rigor already applied to the dissent leg.
risk_of_fix: A pre-fetch/vendoring step reintroduces a network phase whose provenance must be logged or it becomes an unaudited input channel; done carelessly it could pull a different package/data version than the author used and produce a 'reproduction' that silently diverges. An egress allowlist can be over-broad and give false assurance. These additions also raise Act II's complexity and runtime, cutting against the 'cost almost nothing' framing (see S04-F5).

location.section: SKILL.md (entry point & claims) — What makes it trustworthy at scale (s47); README 'Why you can trust a 300-agent run'

They are always on and cost
almost nothing — never traded away for scale.
issue: The 'cost almost nothing' / '~free' framing (also: 'these rails (always on, ~free, never traded for scale)') prices only compute/orchestration overhead and ignores the dominant cost in my jurisdiction: the manufactured confidence a 300-600-agent green light conveys. The rails are genuinely cheap-and-effective against false POSITIVES (fabrication, ungrounded quotes, trivial findings). They are near-absent against false NEGATIVES (S04-F1). That asymmetry makes the green light expensive, not free: a run that misses a real fatal flaw but ships a completeness certificate, multi-angle verification, and 'a world authority on every sub-part' (s24) induces an author/reader to lower scrutiny, which is precisely the 'confident green light laundering a fatal flaw' (s47) the same paragraph promises to prevent. 'Cost almost nothing' is true of the rails' runtime and false of their risk: the expected cost of a missed flaw, weighted by the authority the output carries, is the opposite of negligible.
why_it_matters: Framing the rails as ~free invites running the largest fleet by default and treating its output as a near-guarantee, which is the worst posture given the unguarded false-negative channel. The cost the author should weigh is not tokens but the consequence of an authoritative miss; presenting the rails as costless obscures exactly the trade the failure-modes critic must flag, and overstates C-012/C-051 (the rails make a monumental run trustworthy).
proposed_fix: Re-scope the cost claim: say the rails add little RUNTIME overhead, and replace any implication of costlessness with an explicit statement of residual risk — the rails control false positives and grounding but do not eliminate shared-model false negatives, so the output is a strong critique, not a safety certificate. Pair the 'why you can trust a 300-agent run' section with a 'what this still cannot catch' caveat tied to S04-F1.
risk_of_fix: Adding the caveat blunts the marketing thrust the document is built around and could be read as undercutting the product; it must be worded as honest scope, not self-negation. There is also overlap with the sizing/marketing seat (S03) on the word 'cost' — this finding is scoped to the failure-mode cost (manufactured confidence over an uncaught flaw), not to pricing or audience-sizing language, which is S03's lane.

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution) / DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims)

quote: Invented numbers are structurally impossible.
issue: THE single most likely desk-reject reason. This is the load-bearing trust guarantee of Act II, stated as an absolute impossibility, but the design's own described mechanism is a fallible gate, not a structural impossibility. The mechanism is: Runner executes code, Scribe 'only transcribes a value carrying a provenance token,' and 'the final verifier rejects any number lacking one' (C-059/C-039 context). A provenance token attests that a run occurred and that the value is tagged — it does NOT attest that the digits the Scribe (an LLM) transcribed match the run's actual output. A transposed digit or wrong table cell produces an invented number that still carries a valid token and still passes 'rejects any number lacking one.' The only thing that would catch such drift is the 'numeric-claim reconciliation' / 'Consistency Reconciler' step, which the document itself classifies as a verifier check (s586, §4.6) — i.e., a control that can fail, the opposite of 'structurally impossible.' 'Structurally impossible' asserts a closed proof; the design delivers a strong-but-probabilistic gate. The twin claim C-060 ('This makes fabrication structurally impossible') has the identical defect and should be read together with this one. For a tool whose entire value proposition is trustworthiness, an overclaimed impossibility is not cosmetic — it is the product violating its own grounding rules 4 and 15 (honest labeling, no overclaim) on its highest-stakes sentence.
why_it_matters: A skeptical referee at the target venue (a methods/tooling audience) reaches for the strongest stated guarantee first and tests it. 'Structurally impossible' is falsified by a single Scribe transcription error that carries a valid provenance token — a failure mode the document itself implies exists when it lists numeric reconciliation as a needed verifier and flags 'orphan numbers.' Once the flagship guarantee is shown to be a fallible gate rather than an impossibility, trust in every other absolute in the document collapses. This caps the headline verdict at the floor on this point alone.
proposed_fix: Replace the impossibility claim with an accurate description of the guarantee's actual strength and scope: e.g., 'No number enters the revised paper unless it carries a provenance token tracing to a logged in-session run, and a deterministic consistency check reconciles every transcribed value against that run's output; this makes an UNTRACED number structurally impossible and reduces transcription error to a code-checked residual — it does not eliminate it.' State plainly that the residual failure mode is Scribe transcription of a tagged value, and that the Consistency Reconciler (not a structural impossibility) is what bounds it.
risk_of_fix: The weaker, accurate wording is less marketable and may read as undercutting the Execution-Provenance Wall's selling power; care is needed so it does not over-correct into implying the wall is weak (it is a genuinely strong control — just not an impossibility). Must not delete the true sub-claim that an UNTRACED number cannot enter.

location.section: README.md (public claims) / DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims)

quote:
a completeness audit certifies `covered == total` — "every argument, every word" is a
  *checked invariant*, not a slogan.
issue: The claim defends itself against being a slogan, and that is exactly the hook a skeptical reviewer pulls. The invariant the design can actually check is C-055: 'The union of returns is a sentence-level coverage proof: covered_sentences == total_sentences,' where 'each agent returns a verdict for its whole range.' That certifies that the disjoint sentence tiling was assigned to agents and that each agent emitted a return for its range — i.e., coverage of ATTENTION. It is true essentially by construction (the tiling is defined as disjoint and exhaustive), so 'covered == total' is close to a tautology and certifies nothing about whether 'every argument' was actually examined or examined competently. An agent returning a verdict for a 40-sentence range is not proof that each argument inside it was stress-tested 'to the sentence' (cf. C-003). The document equivocates between coverage-of-assignment (checkable, trivially true) and coverage-of-scrutiny (the thing claimed, not checkable by this invariant), then markets the equivocation as 'a checked invariant, not a slogan.'
why_it_matters: A referee reads 'checked invariant, not a slogan,' inspects what covered==total actually asserts, and concludes it is a slogan wearing an invariant's clothes: a coverage certificate that is green by construction and cannot fail to be green, hence carries no information about review completeness. A completeness certificate that cannot fail is worse than none, because it manufactures false assurance — directly contrary to the tool's stated purpose. This is a clean, quotable desk-reject objection.
proposed_fix: Distinguish the two coverages explicitly: keep 'covered_sentences == total_sentences' but rename/reframe it as a coverage-of-ASSIGNMENT certificate ('every sentence range was assigned to and returned by a reviewing agent') and DROP the inference that this proves 'every argument' was examined. If an argument-level guarantee is wanted, define a separate, falsifiable check (e.g., every load-bearing claim-id in the inventory is cited by >=1 finding or logged 'reviewed, nothing found'), which §2.3/Phase-H partially describes, and make THAT the substantive invariant.
risk_of_fix: The honest reframing makes the marquee 'every argument, every word' guarantee visibly weaker, which may disappoint the intended 'better than any conference' positioning. Risk that authors over-trim and lose the genuinely useful assignment-coverage check; it should be retained, just labeled accurately.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — §6 Build roadmap / §8 Validation track; whole document

issue: Every headline guarantee in the manuscript — 'structurally impossible' (C-040/C-060), 'no fabricated ... — ever' (C-018), 'checked invariant, not a slogan' (C-022), 'keep a 300-600-agent run from laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light' (C-012), 'impeccable revised paper' (C-005) — is ASSERTED, and NONE is demonstrated anywhere in the document. The only evidence apparatus, the 4-arm ablation scoring recall and false-positive rate (C-068), is explicitly scheduled as future, non-blocking work ('Validation track (parallel, non-blocking)'), and the pilot targets (C-069/C-070) are named but not run. There is no reported false-positive rate, no recall number, no worked counterexample showing the rails actually caught a planted flaw, and no demonstration that 'supportive' vs 'brutal' returns an identical must-fix list (the document states this acceptance test, C-026, but shows no run of it). For a manuscript whose entire thesis is 'why you can trust a 300-agent run,' shipping the absolute trust guarantees with zero validating evidence is the most defensible single ground for desk-rejection: the central claim (trustworthiness at scale) is not established by anything in the paper.
why_it_matters: Severity is High and independent of the wording findings above: even if every absolute were reworded honestly, a referee still cannot accept 'this fleet does not launder fatal flaws' without a single demonstration that it doesn't. A trust tool that asks to be trusted on assertion alone fails the most basic referee question — 'show me it works' — and the document's own roadmap concedes the demonstration has not been done. This is the cleanest 'rejected on sight' hook because it needs no internal contradiction to land; the absence of any validation is sufficient.
proposed_fix: Before the absolute guarantees are stated as established, report at least one concrete result from the planned validation track: a recall / false-positive-rate pair on the seeded-flaw + certified-clean benchmark (C-068), at least one worked example where a rail demonstrably caught a planted fabricated number or laundered flaw, and one run of the tone-invariance acceptance test showing identical must-fix lists. Until then, relabel the guarantees as DESIGN INTENT / claimed properties pending the validation track, per grounding rule 15 (honest labeling of a degraded/unvalidated state).
risk_of_fix: Demoting the absolutes to 'design intent pending validation' substantially weakens the document's headline pitch and may read as conceding the tool is unproven (which, on the evidence presented, it is). The risk is purely to marketing strength, not to correctness; the honest labeling is what grounding rule 15 requires.

location.section: SKILL.md (entry point & claims)

quote: impeccable revised paper plus a full replication package
issue: Secondary to the three High overclaims but part of the same pattern a desk editor flags: 'impeccable' is an unqualifiable absolute quality guarantee about an output produced by an LLM tool, asserted in the entry-point description (and echoed as the §3 section title, s561). No review-and-rebuild system can guarantee an 'impeccable' paper; the most it can deliver is a paper with the agreed, verified findings implemented and re-run numbers reconciled. Coming in the same document as 'structurally impossible' and 'no fabricated ... — ever,' 'impeccable' reinforces the reviewer's read of systematic overclaiming and gives a fourth quotable absolute to cite.
why_it_matters: On its own this is a Medium framing issue, not alone fatal; but it materially compounds the desk-reject risk by establishing a pattern (four unhedged absolutes across SKILL.md, README.md, and DESIGN v1). Editors reject documents that read as marketing copy rather than honest engineering, and 'impeccable revised paper' in the first paragraph of the skill description is the tone-setter for that impression.
proposed_fix: Replace 'impeccable' with an accurate descriptor of the output, e.g., 'a revised paper with the agreed findings implemented as tracked changes and every recomputed number reconciled to a logged re-run, plus a full replication package.' Apply the same to the §3 section title.
risk_of_fix: Minimal; the only risk is loss of rhetorical punch in the description/tagline. Ensure the replacement does not accidentally narrow the actual scope of what Act II delivers (tracked edits + re-run + replication package).

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) §6 Build roadmap, item 8; with effect on SKILL.md/README headline claims

issue: Every effectiveness claim in the manuscript is currently unbenchmarked. The document's own theory says the way to know the fleet works is a recall/false-positive measurement: roadmap item 8 promises a '4-arm ablation (one call / +fix-verifier / fixed floor / full fleet) on the author's own papers seeded with planted flaws + certified-clean passages; score recall AND false-positive rate' and says to 'use it to tune the default fan-out and headline the README with a real number'. But that same item is labeled 'Validation track (parallel, non-blocking)' and is explicitly 'not as a gate', i.e. deferred future work — and NO recall number and NO false-positive-rate number appears anywhere in the manuscript. Meanwhile the paper makes strong effectiveness assertions that depend on exactly that missing measurement: 'the rails below are what keep a 300-600-agent run from laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light', 'the largest, most rigorous critique Claude can produce', and 'better than any conference'. The two distinct quantities that would substantiate these — (a) recall (does the fleet catch real fatal flaws?) and (b) false-positive rate (does it avoid manufacturing spurious ones?) — are both promised and both absent. The paper itself elsewhere concedes the false-positive risk is live ('rewards manufacturing marginal false positives'; the finding-killer is added to get 'a real false-positive denominator'), which makes the absence of any measured FPR load-bearing rather than cosmetic.
why_it_matters: This is a design/methodology document whose entire value proposition is effectiveness at scale. The central claim — that a 300-600-agent same-model fleet plus the rails produces trustworthy, conference-beating critique without laundering or manufacturing flaws — is, by the document's own stated standard of proof, established only by a validation that has not been run. A referee cannot accept 'trust a 300-agent run' on the strength of an architecture description alone when the author has named the experiment that would test it and then deferred it. Until at least one recall/FPR number exists, the headline effectiveness claims are unsupported.
proposed_fix: Run the 4-arm ablation (or, minimally, a single recall/FPR pass) before claiming effectiveness, and report both numbers; OR demote the headline claims to explicitly hypothesized/aspirational and move 'better than any conference' / 'largest, most rigorous critique' / the laundering-prevention claim out of the indicative mood until a number backs them. Add an honest 'Validation status: not yet run' line wherever effectiveness is asserted (consistent with grounding rule 15).
risk_of_fix: Softening the headline claims weakens the marketing/positioning and could understate a tool that may in fact perform well; conversely, rushing a thin ablation and headlining a single noisy number could overstate effectiveness. The fix should add the caveat now and the number later, not invent a number.

location.section: Act II (ATELIER) claims across README s166 and DESIGN v1 §3 / §8; examples/ directory

issue: Act II — which the paper names as its differentiator ('Phase 2 (running the author's .do/.R/.py and handing back a corrected, reproducing manuscript) is the moat — nothing in the lineage does it') — has no end-to-end demonstration anywhere. The strongest Act II guarantees are asserted purely as architecture: 'clean-room-replicates it to prove it reproduces', 'Independent clean-room replication ... non-reproducing package can't be marked final', and 'This makes fabrication structurally impossible'. None of these is shown actually holding on a real paper. The document even names a pilot with real data and code for exactly this purpose ('Primary: optimal_inflation/ ... a real replication package (56 .py, 30 .csv, .dta, .do, .R) ... Exercises BOTH phases'), yet no Act II run, no regenerated table/figure under the Execution-Provenance Wall, no baseline-reproduction result, and no clean-room replication outcome is reported. The only worked example present (examples/self-audit/) reaches the cartography stage (claim inventory, sentence map, precis) and stops — it never reaches Act II at all.
why_it_matters: The moat claim and the reproducibility/anti-fabrication guarantees are the half of the tool that distinguishes it from mad-research and that justify the 'rebuilds the paper and its replication package' promise. A guarantee that 'fabrication is structurally impossible' and that the package 'reproduces' is an empirical claim about a running system; with zero executed Act II evidence — on a pilot the author says is already in hand — these guarantees are undemonstrated. A referee would treat an unexercised differentiating capability as a claim, not a result.
proposed_fix: Execute Act II once on the optimal_inflation pilot and include the artifacts the design promises (baseline-reproduction diff, at least one provenance-tagged regenerated number/figure, a MAP.md, and a clean-room replication log), or explicitly label every Act II guarantee as 'designed, not yet demonstrated' and remove the indicative 'proves it reproduces' / 'structurally impossible' phrasing until a run exists.
risk_of_fix: A single pilot run could surface that some guarantee does not hold end-to-end (e.g. baseline does not reproduce), which is itself valuable but may force claim retraction; labeling-only (without running) preserves honesty but leaves the moat unproven and may invite the same criticism at review.

location.section: helpers/verification_panel.md (the multi-angle gate) s389; SKILL.md/README 'trust a 300-agent run'

issue: The multi-angle verification panel is the load-bearing rail for everything that is NOT a quote — logical-validity, factual-literature, severity-calibration, decision-relevance, steelman-charity — yet the manuscript gives no demonstration that running N independent SAME-MODEL verifiers actually decorrelates errors. The panel's redundancy is specified numerically ('Run >=3 verifiers on the hard-gate angles and >=1 on each soft angle' at thorough; 'the full 7-angle panel, with 2 independent verifiers per angle (majority within an angle)' at exhaustive/monumental), and the whole trust story ('Why you can trust a 300-agent run') rests on it. But the document itself identifies the exact failure mode that would defeat this — 'An LLM verifier shares the hallucination it is checking' — and then closes it ONLY for quotes (via the deterministic quote_gate.py script). For every non-quote angle the verifier is itself an LLM, and the residual correlated-error rate (the probability that K blind Claude verifiers share the same blind spot and all pass a wrong finding, or all reject a correct one) is never measured or even estimated. There is no evidence the panel catches errors a single pass would miss.
why_it_matters: If same-model verifiers are substantially correlated on the non-quote angles, then '>=3 verifiers' and '2 per angle, majority within an angle' provide far less protection than the prose implies, and the claim that the panel keeps a large fleet from 'laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light' is unsupported precisely where it matters most (the judgments that cannot be reduced to a script). This is a rail asserted without any demonstration that it holds; it is the empirical premise underneath the central trust claim.
proposed_fix: Add a measurement of verifier decorrelation for the non-quote angles (e.g. report, on seeded findings, how often added independent verifiers change the panel verdict, and the panel's residual error rate vs a single pass), and report it alongside the trust claims; OR explicitly scope the trust claim to what the deterministic gates guarantee (quotes, and Act II numeric provenance/consistency) and caveat that the LLM-judged angles share a model and their independence is assumed, not measured.
risk_of_fix: Measuring decorrelation could reveal weak independence and undercut the 'trust a 300-agent run' headline; the redesign or caveat could read as the tool conceding its core weakness. But asserting independence without evidence is the larger risk. The measurement must not itself be graded only by correlated LLM judges.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) §7 Pilot targets, 'Primary: optimal_inflation/'

issue: The manuscript states it already has a ready-made, low-cost validation in hand and still does not run or report it. Of the optimal_inflation pilot it says: 'the existing human edit patches are a free recall/false-positive benchmark (run Act I blind to them, then diff)'. A blind Act I pass diffed against the existing manuscript_edits.patch / reppackage_edits.patch would yield exactly the recall/FPR evidence the headline claims need, at the cost of one Act I run — no new data collection, no flaw-seeding, no ablation infrastructure. That diff result is absent from the manuscript. This is distinct from the formal 4-arm ablation (F1): it is the cheapest available check, the author asserts the benchmark exists, and even it was left undone.
why_it_matters: The gap in F1 might be excused as 'the full ablation is expensive future work', but here the document concedes a free benchmark is sitting on disk. The absence of even this cheap, author-acknowledged recall/FPR check makes the unbenchmarked-effectiveness problem materially harder to wave off, and a referee will read 'free benchmark' + 'no result reported' as a conspicuous omission.
proposed_fix: Run Act I blind on optimal_inflation, diff against the existing human edit patches, and report the resulting recall and false-positive counts (with the obvious caveats about a single paper and patch-as-ground-truth); cite that number wherever effectiveness is claimed. If it cannot be run before release, state explicitly that the benchmark exists but has not yet been executed.
risk_of_fix: Human edit patches are an imperfect gold standard (they include stylistic edits and omit issues the humans missed), so a naive recall/FPR diff could mislead in either direction; the report must frame the patches as a proxy, not ground truth. Judging whether this benchmark is well-designed is out of this seat's scope (S08) — this finding only flags that it was not run.

location.section: SKILL.md Depth tiers table & DESIGN v1 §2.2 tiers table (~agent-instantiations); README 'trust a 300-agent run'

issue: The seat counts and fleet-sizing figures are presented as if calibrated, but no derivation, measurement, or sensitivity evidence supports any of them. The tiers assert specific magnitudes — 'quick 6-8', 'thorough 12-18 ~40-60', 'exhaustive 25-40 ... ~120-180', 'monumental 60-120+ ... ~300-600' — and the README headlines 'trust a 300-agent run', yet nothing shows that more seats find more true flaws, that the marginal flaw-yield curve justifies these counts, or that the default 'thorough' tier is the right operating point. The document itself concedes the calibration does not yet exist: the (unrun) ablation is the thing that would 'tune the default fan-out'. So the entire sizing scheme — the most visible quantitative content in the paper — is currently unjustified.

Numbers presented in a table read as engineered defaults; absent any yield-vs-size evidence they are unsupported guesses, and the claim that bigger tiers are 'better' (up to 'better than any conference') has no measured basis. A referee will ask 'why 12-18 and not 4?' and find no answer in the paper.
proposed_fix: Either report the flaw-yield-vs-fan-out evidence from the ablation that the paper says will 'tune the default fan-out' (even a single curve on one pilot), or relabel the tier counts as provisional engineering defaults pending validation rather than calibrated recommendations, and avoid implying that larger tiers are demonstrably better until measured.
risk_of_fix: A yield curve from one or two papers may not generalize and could entrench an arbitrary default with a false veneer of rigor; labeling the counts provisional is safe but concedes the headline sizing is not yet evidence-based.

location.section: README s155 / DESIGN v1 §2.3 (coverage invariant); examples/self-audit/ artifacts (minor notes, folded)

issue: Folded minor absence notes, each a guarantee asserted as 'checked' but with no executed artifact demonstrating it: (1) The coverage invariant is claimed as proven ('a completeness audit certifies covered == total — "every argument, every word" is a checked invariant, not a slogan' / 'The union of returns is a sentence-level coverage proof: covered_sentences == total_sentences'), but no completeness certificate or green coverage ledger is presented anywhere; the self-audit example contains a sentence_map.json but no audited 'covered == total' result, so the invariant is specified, not yet checked-and-shown. Individually these are not fatal, but together they reinforce the pattern that the manuscript's guarantees are architectural assertions awaiting their first executed evidence.
