location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — §6 Build roadmap item 8 (Validation track)

quote: 4-arm ablation (one call / +fix-verifier / fixed floor / full fleet) on the author's own papers seeded with planted flaws + certified-clean passages; score recall AND false-positive rate
issue: The false-positive-rate denominator is circular. FPR is to be computed against 'certified-clean passages', but a passage being genuinely flaw-free is exactly the property the tool exists to adjudicate, and the design never says who certifies cleanliness or how independently. If the tool flags something inside a passage the author pre-labeled 'clean', there is no way to distinguish a true false positive from a real flaw the author's certification missed — so every such flag is scored as a tool error by construction. The FPR number this instrument yields is therefore not a measurement of the tool's false-positive behavior; it measures agreement with the author's own (unvalidated, same-team) cleanliness labels. This is the headline number the roadmap intends to publish ('headline the README with a real number'), so an uninterpretable denominator contaminates a public, load-bearing claim.
why_it_matters: FPR is half of the only quantitative validation the tool proposes for its core promise (not 'laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light'). A circular clean denominator makes the published FPR uninterpretable and potentially self-flattering: the tool is graded against labels produced by the same party that built it, with no independent ground truth.
proposed_fix: Define the clean denominator independently of the tool's authors: e.g., passages drawn from papers that subsequently cleared peer review at the target venue AND were certified flaw-free by ≥2 blinded domain experts who did not build the tool, with disagreements adjudicated and logged; treat any tool flag inside a 'clean' passage as adjudicated by those independent experts (real flaw vs false positive), not auto-scored as error. Report inter-certifier agreement so the denominator's own reliability is visible.
risk_of_fix: Independent expert certification is expensive and may shrink the usable clean set, lowering statistical power; experts may themselves miss subtle flaws, so 'certified clean' remains probabilistic — the fix reduces but cannot eliminate denominator uncertainty, and the residual must be disclosed rather than hidden.

tradition: Empirical methods evaluation; benchmark & metrology design

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — §6 Build roadmap item 8 (Validation track)

quote: on the author's own papers seeded with planted flaws + certified-clean passages; score recall AND false-positive rate
issue: The recall arm is exposed to a teaching-to-the-test confound that the design never controls for. Flaws are 'planted' with no statement that the flaw author is blinded to, or independent from, the team that built the seat roster, the floor, and the verifiers. A fleet whose seats are designed by the same people who plant the flaws will preferentially recall the flaw archetypes its designers find salient; recall measured this way estimates self-consistency, not detection of the subtle, adversarial flaws the tool claims to catch in the wild. The design also specifies no difficulty stratification (obvious vs subtle planted flaws) and no realism criterion, so a high recall could be driven entirely by easy, on-distribution plants.
why_it_matters: Recall is the other half of the headline validation. If planted flaws are authored by the tool's own builders without blinding or a realism/difficulty taxonomy, the recall figure overstates real-world detection — exactly the failure mode (false confidence at scale) the tool is marketed to prevent.
proposed_fix: Have planted flaws authored by an independent party blinded to the roster/floor/verifier design; stratify plants by a pre-registered difficulty/realism taxonomy (e.g., surface typo → mis-stated stat → subtle identification/leakage flaw) and report recall per stratum, not pooled; include a held-out flaw class never shown to the tool's designers during tuning. Report recall separately from the tuning set used to set the default fan-out so the headline number is not computed on the data used to tune.
risk_of_fix: Independent blinded flaw authoring is costly and may yield fewer plants, widening confidence intervals; an over-aggressive 'subtle' stratum could push recall low in a way that understates performance on the flaws users actually care about — so per-stratum reporting (not a single pooled number) is essential to avoid trading one misleading summary for another.

tradition: Empirical methods evaluation; benchmark & metrology design

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — §7 Pilot targets (Primary: optimal_inflation)

quote: the existing human edit patches are a free recall/false-positive benchmark (run Act I blind to them, then diff)
issue: Existing human edit patches are not a valid recall/FPR gold standard, and the design treats them as one. A referee/author patch records the changes those particular humans chose to make — it is neither an exhaustive enumeration of the paper's flaws (real flaws they missed are absent) nor a pure flaw list (it also contains style, wording, and venue-formatting edits that are not 'flaws' at all). Diffing Act I against this patch therefore mis-measures both axes: tool findings absent from the patch are scored as false positives even when they are genuine flaws the humans overlooked, and patch entries the tool did not raise are scored as misses even when they are non-flaw stylistic edits outside the tool's remit. 'Recall' and 'false-positive rate' computed against an incidental human patch are not the quantities the labels claim.
why_it_matters: This is the only 'free' benchmark named for the primary pilot, and it is offered as if it directly yields recall and FPR. Built on a non-gold-standard reference, those numbers would systematically understate recall and overstate FPR (or vice versa) in unknown proportion, and could be published as the tool's empirical validation.
proposed_fix: Treat the human patch as a partial reference, not ground truth: (i) have an independent adjudicator label each patch hunk as flaw-fix vs non-flaw (style/format) and exclude non-flaw hunks from the recall denominator; (ii) adjudicate tool findings absent from the patch as true-flaw-missed-by-humans vs genuine-false-positive rather than auto-scoring them as FP; (iii) report 'agreement with the human patch' as a descriptive concordance statistic distinct from recall/FPR against an adjudicated reference.
risk_of_fix: Manual adjudication reintroduces subjective judgment and labor the 'free benchmark' was meant to avoid; an adjudicator who sees the tool's output may anchor on it (adjudication should be blind to which side proposed each item). Done carelessly the adjudication itself becomes a new uncontrolled labeler.

tradition: Empirical methods evaluation; benchmark & metrology design

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — §6 Build roadmap item 8 (Validation track)

issue: The 4-arm ablation is specified as a list of arms but not as a measurement protocol. The design states no acceptance/decision criterion (what recall and FPR delta between 'one call' and '+fix-verifier', or between 'fixed floor' and 'full fleet', would count as the marginal rail 'working'); no number of papers / planted flaws (n); no uncertainty quantification (the rubric forbids confidence scores, but confidence intervals on an empirical recall/FPR are descriptive statistics, not the prohibited acceptance-probability — their absence is a real gap); and no handling of the multiplicity introduced by comparing four nested arms on the same seeded corpus. It also does not state that the arms are run independently — same papers, same seeds, and a shared orchestrator across nested supersets invite cross-arm leakage (later arms reusing earlier arms' cached findings), which would bias the marginal-value estimate of each rail. As written the ablation cannot yield a defensible 'the fix-verifier adds X recall' conclusion.
why_it_matters: The ablation's whole purpose is to attribute marginal detection value to specific rails (fix-verifier, floor, full fleet) and to 'tune the default fan-out'. Without a pre-stated effect metric, an n, uncertainty bounds, and an independence guarantee across arms, any reported delta is uninterpretable and the fan-out tuning rests on noise — a methods-paper-grade design defect for the tool's central empirical claim.
proposed_fix: Pre-register the ablation as a protocol: define the primary estimand (e.g., marginal recall and marginal FPR of each rail vs the next-simpler arm), fix n papers and n planted flaws with a power/precision rationale, report confidence intervals (descriptive, not acceptance odds) and correct for the four-arm multiplicity, and guarantee arm independence (fresh orchestrator state and no shared finding cache per arm; if seeds are reused for paired comparison, state it and use paired analysis deliberately).
risk_of_fix: A fully pre-registered, adequately powered ablation is a substantial undertaking that could delay release; over-formalizing a tuning experiment (treating it as a confirmatory trial) risks implying more rigor than a fan-out-tuning exercise needs — the protocol should be proportionate and labeled as tuning, consistent with 'not as a gate'.

tradition: Empirical methods evaluation; benchmark & metrology design

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — §4 integrity rails, item 10

quote: **Independent clean-room replication** of the final package (pinned, seeded, hermetic); non-reproducing package can't be marked final.
issue: The gate predicate 'reproducing' / 'non-reproducing' is never operationally defined, so the rule 'non-reproducing package can't be marked final' is not decidable as written. The only operationalization given (in §3.5: "`00_run_all` reproduces embedded figures/tables") still leaves 'reproduces' undefined: bit-for-bit identity, or numerical agreement within a tolerance? For any stochastic analysis — even with seeds set — differences in BLAS/LAPACK builds, library/compiler versions, floating-point summation order, and OS routinely perturb low-order digits, so a strict byte/identity test will fail on perfectly correct packages, while no stated tolerance means there is no objective threshold to declare success. A pass/fail gate built on an undefined comparison is unfalsifiable and will be adjudicated ad hoc by an LLM, which defeats the 'deterministic gate' philosophy the document elsewhere insists on.
why_it_matters: This rail is a headline trust guarantee ('clean-room-replicates it to prove it reproduces', C-025/C-065) and a final-status gate. If 'reproduces' has no defined tolerance and comparison method, the guarantee is either vacuous (any wiggle passes) or impossible (any digit drift fails), and 'final' status rests on an unspecified judgment call rather than a deterministic check.
proposed_fix: Specify the reproduction predicate deterministically: for each artifact class define the comparison (e.g., exact match for integers/counts; published-precision or explicit relative/absolute tolerance for floating-point; structural/perceptual comparison for figures), the tolerance values, and the seed/environment assumptions; emit a machine-checkable reproduction report (per-number pass/fail against tolerance) so the 'can't be marked final' gate is a code decision, not an LLM's eyeball.
risk_of_fix: Choosing tolerances is itself a scientific judgment — too loose hides real non-reproduction, too tight fails correct packages on benign numeric noise; tolerances appropriate for one analysis class may be wrong for another, so a single global tolerance would be a new error. The predicate must be per-artifact and disclosed, which adds specification burden.

tradition: Empirical methods evaluation; benchmark & metrology design

location.section: README.md (public claims) — Act II ATELIER

quote: clean-room-replicates it to prove it reproduces.
issue: The instrument proves a weaker thing than the claim states. As specified (§3.5: "`00_run_all` reproduces embedded figures/tables"; §3.6: outputs are 'real logged re-run outputs'), the clean-room re-run regenerates the SAME artifacts that Act II's own logged runs just produced and embedded — i.e., it demonstrates the package is internally self-consistent and re-executable, which for seeded deterministic code is close to tautological. It does NOT independently establish that the package reproduces the numbers in the author's ORIGINAL manuscript: those are validated separately by the baseline-reproduction gate (§3.3), and once Act II has propagated re-run outputs into the revised paper, the clean-room step is checking the package against the package, not against the published record. 'Prove it reproduces' (unqualified) reads as the strong, externally meaningful claim; the machinery delivers the narrow internal one. Additionally a single clean-room instance shows determinism on one environment, not portability/reproducibility across environments, which is what 'replication' connotes to AEA/TOP reviewers.
why_it_matters: Reproducibility is the moat the tool markets ('Phase 2 ... is the moat'). Conflating 'the package regenerates its own freshly-computed outputs' with 'the package reproduces the manuscript's results' overstates the guarantee a user receives; a package can pass this gate while still not matching the paper's originally reported numbers if Act II silently changed them.
proposed_fix: Split and scope the claim: (a) state that the clean-room step proves the replication package re-executes and regenerates its own embedded outputs (internal reproducibility), and (b) report the SEPARATE comparison of those outputs against the manuscript's reported values (which may differ post-revision, and if so must be flagged as a changed-number under the integrity rails). Where 'replication' (cross-environment) is claimed, run the package in at least one environment distinct from the one that produced it; otherwise label the guarantee 'deterministic re-execution', not 'replication'.
risk_of_fix: A second independent environment adds infrastructure (e.g., container vs host, or a different OS) and may surface benign cross-platform numeric drift that needs the tolerance policy from S08-F5 to interpret; over-qualifying the README could read as walking back a genuine strength — the wording must stay accurate without underselling the real internal-reproducibility guarantee.

tradition: Empirical methods evaluation; benchmark & metrology design

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) — §4 integrity rails, item 7 (Acceptance test)

quote: **Acceptance test:** same paper under "supportive" vs neutral framing → identical must-fix list.
issue: The tone-invariance acceptance test is specified against the wrong comparator relative to the claim it is meant to certify. The README and the constitution define the property as invariance between the two register EXTREMES — "the same paper reviewed 'supportively' or 'brutally' returns the same must-fix list" (README, C-026) and "'supportive' vs. 'brutal' framing must return an identical must-fix list" (shared_grounding_rules rule 4). But the integrity-rail acceptance test that the build must pass compares "supportive vs neutral framing". Supportive-vs-neutral is a strictly weaker test than supportive-vs-brutal: passing it does not establish invariance against the brutal register, which is precisely the extreme that the `brutal` mode exercises and that most plausibly perturbs severity. The instrument therefore does not test the invariance the tool advertises and a 'brutal' run could violate the advertised guarantee while still passing the stated acceptance test.
why_it_matters: Tone-invariance of the must-fix list is a load-bearing trust claim made in both public-facing files. An acceptance test whose comparator (neutral) differs from the advertised comparator (brutal) can certify 'pass' while the advertised property (brutal == supportive) is untested — a gap between the guarantee and the check that validates it.
proposed_fix: Align the acceptance test with the advertised claim: make the binding comparison supportive vs brutal (the two extremes), and optionally add neutral as a third point. State a single canonical comparator across SKILL/README/constitution/rails so the three files stop disagreeing on what is compared.
risk_of_fix: Testing the extremes is the harder bar and is more likely to surface real (or noise-driven) list differences, which could block a build — but that is the correct behavior if the advertised invariance does not hold; the risk is mistaking sampling noise for a tone effect, which is exactly why the control in S08-F8 is needed alongside this fix.

tradition: Empirical methods evaluation; benchmark & metrology design

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution) — rule 4 (Severity is tone-invariant), and README 'No confidence scores. Severity is tone-invariant'

issue: The tone-invariance test, as defined, cannot attribute a difference to tone because it has no control for run-to-run nondeterminism. The metric is identity of the must-fix LIST across two register conditions, but (i) 'identical list' is itself undefined — same finding ids? same count? same severities? same ordering? — and (ii) the fleet is a stochastic LLM ensemble, so two runs at the SAME register will already differ (different seats firing, different marginal findings) purely from sampling variation. Without a same-register test-retest baseline (run the paper twice under identical framing to quantify the no-treatment difference), a supportive-vs-brutal difference confounds the tone effect with ordinary nondeterminism, and an observed identity cannot be distinguished from coincidence. As a measurement of tone-invariance the test is missing its control arm and its operational definition of 'identical', so a 'pass' or 'fail' is uninterpretable.
why_it_matters: This acceptance test is the document's own proof that severity is tone-invariant — the property that justifies running a `brutal` register at all without distorting the must-fix set. If the test has no nondeterminism control and no defined match criterion, it can neither validate invariance (a 'pass' may be luck) nor diagnose a violation (a 'fail' may be sampling noise), so the central tone-decoupling guarantee is asserted but not actually testable as specified.
proposed_fix: Define 'identical must-fix list' precisely (recommend: identical SET of must-fix finding ids at identical severity, ordering-exempt) and add a same-register test-retest baseline: run the paper k times under one register to estimate the within-register list-difference distribution, then accept tone-invariance only if the cross-register difference is within that null band. Report the comparison on stable finding identity (e.g., matched by quote+locator), not raw text, so sampling-driven wording changes don't masquerade as tone effects.
risk_of_fix: Repeated multi-run testing multiplies an already expensive run; if k is small the null band is noisy and the test is underpowered; an overly permissive 'within the null band' rule could let a genuine tone effect hide inside large nondeterminism — so the within-register variance must be reported, not just thresholded, and reducing fleet nondeterminism (lower temperature / fixed seeds where possible) may be needed for the test to have power.

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution)

quote:
This
   is the only thing that makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws.
issue: This is the paper's single most emphatic decorrelation claim (rule 5; C-033), and it rests on a category error. Commit-and-reveal isolation removes only the correlation introduced by inter-agent message-passing (one seat anchoring on another). It does nothing about the correlation that matters here: every seat is drawn from the SAME Claude distribution, so the draws are identically distributed. Statistical independence (no communication) and non-identical-distribution (genuinely different error structure) are different properties; isolation buys the former and leaves the latter untouched. A blind spot in the training distribution -- a class of flaw the model systematically cannot see, or a misconception it systematically holds -- is a property of the common generative process, not of the dependence structure, and appears in every isolated draw with probability ~1. So isolation makes the fleet N INDEPENDENT draws but they remain N IDENTICALLY-DISTRIBUTED draws; for the shared-blind-spot failure mode (the only one that can launder a fatal flaw past a 300-agent fleet), isolation is the wrong lever and the word 'only' makes the overclaim exact.
why_it_matters: C-033 is load-bearing for the entire trust proposition: it is the asserted reason a same-model fleet is not just N correlated draws. If isolation cannot touch shared-distribution error, the central justification for believing a Claude-only fleet decorrelates is unsupported, and the headline 'more than any conference' / 'trust a 300-agent run' claims inherit that gap.
proposed_fix: Stop claiming isolation is what makes the fleet more than N correlated draws. State precisely what commit-and-reveal does (eliminates inter-agent anchoring/herding) and explicitly concede what it does NOT do (cannot reduce error shared across draws from one model). Relocate the real decorrelation hope to mechanisms that change the conditioning or the model (opposed objective functions, the external non-Claude leg) and label residual shared-blind-spot risk as an acknowledged, unmitigated limitation pending the planted-flaw validation.
risk_of_fix: Conceding this narrows the marketing claim and could read as undermining the product's premise; the author must be careful not to overcorrect into implying the fleet adds nothing (it still removes herding and broadens coverage, which are real).

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution)

quote:
An LLM verifier shares the
    hallucination it is checking, so this gate is a **script**, fail-closed.
issue: The paper states this principle to justify making the quote-gate a deterministic script -- conceding that a same-model verifier shares the error it audits. But the verification panel then relies on Claude subagents for five of its seven Act-I angles (logical-validity, factual-literature, severity-calibration, decision-relevance, steelman-charity); only quote-locator (and, in Act II, numeric-provenance and consistency) is scriptable. By the paper's own stated principle, those five Claude verifiers share precisely the hallucinations they are meant to catch. The architecture solves the correlated-error problem only for the narrow class a script can handle and then claims general protection. This is a contradiction internal to the manuscript, not an external critique: rule 10 indicts the panel that the README leans on to certify trust.
why_it_matters: C-012 asserts these rails 'keep a 300-600-agent run from laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light.' If the model that produces a flawed finding is also the model that logic-checks it, factual-checks it, and steelmans it, a shared blind spot survives the entire panel -- the verifier cannot catch what it cannot represent. The paper's flagship trust mechanism is, by its own logic, ineffective against exactly the failure (shared-distribution error) that a same-model fleet is most exposed to.
proposed_fix: Acknowledge that LLM-backed verification angles share the proposer's distribution and therefore cannot independently catch shared-blind-spot errors; restrict the strong 'launder-proof' language to the script-backed gates (quote, numeric-provenance, consistency). For the judgment angles, either route them through a different model/provider (extending the external leg from optional to load-bearing) or downgrade the claim to 'catches independent slips and inconsistencies' rather than fatal-flaw protection.
risk_of_fix: Making non-Claude verification load-bearing conflicts with the 'Claude-only' identity and the confidentiality/no-train constraints noted for external calls; the author may not be able to fully close the gap, in which case the honest move is to scope the trust claim down rather than to add a mechanism.

location.section: README.md (public claims)

quote:
instantiated with *opposed objective functions* (one
  "find the fatal flaw," its rival "find the strongest defensible version"). Real
  disagreement, not disciplinary costume.
issue: This asserts a disjunction (the disagreement is real, NOT costume) and selects the favorable horn with no supporting evidence. Opposed objective functions condition one and the same Claude distribution on two instructions; this re-weights which outputs are sampled but cannot conjure a capability, fact, or failure-mode the base model lacks. On any region where the model is systematically wrong or blind, both heads agree silently: the 'find the flaw' head does not surface the flaw it cannot see, and the 'find the strongest version' head cheerfully defends it. The visible disagreement is real only on the sub-manifold the model can already represent; on shared blind spots the two heads converge, which is the case that matters. So 'real disagreement, not disciplinary costume' may itself be costume -- both heads are one model -- and the paper provides nothing to distinguish genuine opposed-incentive diversity from two conditioned reads of the same prior.
why_it_matters: Rule 6 elevates 'decorrelate by rival objective function, not job title' to a non-negotiable and the README sells it as what makes disagreement real. If opposed prompts cannot decorrelate shared-distribution error, then the second pillar of the decorrelation story (after isolation, F1) also fails to support the 'more than N correlated draws' conclusion, and the contrast with mad-research's genuine cross-MODEL disagreement is overstated.
proposed_fix: Replace the asserted dichotomy with a calibrated claim: opposed objective functions reduce the convergence-by-agreeableness and shared-framing failure modes and broaden the search, but cannot decorrelate errors rooted in the shared model's knowledge/blind spots. Either present the planted-flaw ablation evidence that the two heads actually diverge on real flaws, or soften 'Real disagreement, not disciplinary costume' to a hypothesis the validation track is designed to test.
risk_of_fix: Softening the headline weakens a key selling point versus mad-research; overcorrection risk is implying the rival-objective design is worthless, when it plausibly does suppress sycophantic convergence -- the claim should be narrowed, not abandoned.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) -- sec 6 build roadmap item 8 / sec 8

issue: Nowhere does the manuscript present any executed measurement -- or even a BLOCKING validation -- that the single-model fleet decorrelates or that the rails prevent laundering. The one test capable of bearing on it (the 4-arm 'one call / +fix-verifier / fixed floor / full fleet' ablation on planted flaws plus certified-clean passages, scoring recall AND false-positive rate) is explicitly 'parallel, non-blocking,' is meant only to 'tune the default fan-out and headline the README with a real number -- not as a gate,' and the document reports no result from it. So the central efficacy claims (C-033 'more than N correlated draws'; C-012 the rails stop a 300-600-agent run from 'laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light') are asserted, load-bearing, and unfalsified by anything in the manuscript. This is compounded by the run's framing: the manuscript IS the tool auditing itself (self-audit), so the single in-the-document demonstration of the fleet is maximally exposed to the very shared-blind-spot failure it needs to rule out -- a same-model fleet reviewing a same-model design cannot detect a blind spot it shares with the document's author-model.
why_it_matters: The decorrelation and anti-laundering claims are the load-bearing justification for trusting a 300-600-agent same-model run; with no executed evidence and the only proposed test deferred and non-blocking, the strongest claims in the paper rest on assertion. Until the ablation runs, a reader cannot distinguish 'the fleet catches more' from 'the fleet generates N correlated confirmations.' A claim this central, presented as a guarantee, should not ship validated only by the tool's own self-review.
proposed_fix: Either run the planted-flaw / certified-clean ablation and report decorrelation-relevant numbers (e.g., shared-miss rate across isolated seats; recall on planted flaws the base single-call misses; false-positive rate) before asserting 'more than N correlated draws,' OR demote C-033/C-012 from asserted guarantees to explicitly unvalidated design hypotheses, and disclose that the self-audit demonstration cannot test shared-blind-spot resistance because reviewer and reviewed share a model.
risk_of_fix: Running the ablation is real work and may return an unflattering number; demoting the claims weakens the pitch. The honest minimum (labeling the claims unvalidated and disclosing the self-audit's blind-spot limitation) is cheap and carries little risk beyond softened marketing.

location.section: prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution) -- rule 6

quote:
Inter-seat overlap is reported as a
   **diagnostic** the author weighs
issue: The only instrument the paper offers for monitoring fleet correlation measures overlap of what seats FOUND. By construction this is blind to the failure mode the decorrelation claim must guard against: correlation of what seats all MISSED. Two isolated same-model seats that share a blind spot will each fail to raise the same true flaw; their found-finding sets can look perfectly NON-overlapping (low measured overlap, read as healthy diversity) while their miss-sets are identical. The overlap diagnostic therefore cannot detect monoculture in the dimension that matters; a reassuring overlap number is consistent with a fleet that is N correlated draws on every flaw it cannot see.
why_it_matters: The paper points to the inter-seat overlap diagnostic as the author's tool for weighing correlation. If that instrument is structurally insensitive to shared misses, the author is given false comfort: the metric most likely to be cited as evidence of diversity is exactly the one that cannot see the correlated-error problem.
proposed_fix: State explicitly that the overlap diagnostic measures redundancy of detections, not correlation of misses, and add a shared-miss estimator from the planted-flaw harness (fraction of planted flaws missed by ALL isolated seats) as the actual decorrelation metric. Caution the author in the text not to read low found-overlap as evidence of blind-spot diversity.
risk_of_fix: A shared-miss metric requires planted ground truth, so it only exists once the validation track runs; until then the fix is honest labeling of the diagnostic's scope, which carries no correctness risk.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) -- sec 4 item 9

quote: external dissent leg** ("what did *all* Claude seats miss?") operating on abstracted findings, never raw data
issue: The phrase 'what did ALL Claude seats miss?' is the paper's own admission that the single-model fleet has a shared miss-set -- i.e., that F1/F3 are real risks. But the only mechanism aimed at it is structurally too weak to detect it on three counts the text states: it is optional and 'skipped+disclosed if no compliant endpoint'; it is explicitly 'lower-weight'; and it operates on 'abstracted findings, never raw data' (and never the manuscript). A blind spot lives precisely in what the fleet FAILED to flag; an external leg that sees only the abstracted findings the fleet already produced -- not the paper itself -- has no surface on which to recover an un-flagged flaw. The mitigation is gated, down-weighted, and blind to the very artifact (the manuscript) where the shared miss would have to be caught.
why_it_matters: This is the one place the architecture concedes the monoculture problem and gestures at a cross-model remedy. Because that remedy is optional, lower-weight by design, and cannot see the paper, the concession is unmatched by a working countermeasure -- which sharpens, rather than relieves, the unsupported status of C-033/C-012.
proposed_fix: If the external dissent leg is to count as the monoculture countermeasure, give it the manuscript (or representative excerpts) so it can find un-flagged flaws, not just re-weight already-found ones; and present it as a measured contributor (how many net-new High/Med findings it surfaces) rather than an optional, abstracted, lower-weight afterthought. Otherwise, do not let its existence support any claim that the fleet's shared blind spots are covered.
risk_of_fix: Sending the manuscript to a non-Claude model collides with the confidentiality / no-train / 'never send raw data externally' constraints the paper itself sets; the author may legitimately keep the leg restricted -- in which case the fix is to drop any implication that shared blind spots are mitigated, not to widen the leg.

location.section: README.md (public claims)

quote:
Real
  disagreement, not disciplinary costume.
issue: I defend this claim in its strongest form and it survives in principle: conditioning a same-weights head on an opposed objective function ('find the fatal flaw' vs 'find the strongest defensible version') genuinely steers its search direction, so two such heads are not i.i.d. draws from one prior and the design is more than a disciplinary 'costume'. That defensible core is real. What does NOT survive is the indicative mood: 'Real disagreement' is stated as an achieved property of the output, but the manuscript offers no evidence that opposed-objective heads on one model actually produce decorrelated findings. The only instrument that would establish it — the recall/false-positive ablation and the inter-seat overlap diagnostic — is described elsewhere as future and explicitly 'not as a gate' ('score recall AND false-positive rate ... headline the README with a real number — not as a gate.'). So the claim asserts demonstrated decorrelation while the mechanism's efficacy is, by the document's own roadmap, still unmeasured. This is the central honest weakness in my jurisdiction: the mechanism is sound to *hypothesize*, not yet earned the right to *assert*.
why_it_matters: Decorrelation is the load-bearing justification for the whole fleet (it is what rule 6 cites to treat convergence as signal rather than redundancy, and what C-033 calls 'the only thing that makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws'). If a reader takes 'Real disagreement' as established fact rather than design intent, every downstream 'two seats agree => stronger signal' inference inherits an unproven premise. A public-facing tool stating an unvalidated efficacy claim in the indicative is a fixable overclaim that a careful referee would flag.
proposed_fix: Re-mood the claim from achieved fact to design hypothesis plus a falsifiable test: e.g. 'Designed for real disagreement, not disciplinary costume — and measured: the inter-seat overlap diagnostic and the recall/false-positive ablation report whether opposed-objective heads actually decorrelate, with the number published once the validation track lands.' Keep the strong mechanism language but bind it to the diagnostic that already exists in the design.
risk_of_fix: Softening the headline could read as hedging and slightly dull the marketing punch; if over-hedged it could undersell a mechanism that is genuinely sound in principle. Keep the assertive mechanism description, change only the epistemic status verb.

location.section: shared_grounding_rules.md (the constitution) rule 6 / DESIGN v1 §2.2 / README.md s152-s153

issue: Even on the most generous reading, the design is silent about a residual-correlation confound it cannot rule out. Opposed objective functions decorrelate the *search direction*, but every head still shares: the same base weights, the same shared_grounding_rules constitution, the same locked rubric.md, the same deterministic quote_gate, and a common Casting Director prompt that wrote all their jurisdictions. A blind spot in any of these shared priors — a class of flaw the base model cannot perceive, or a false-positive pattern the rubric induces — is shared by EVERY seat irrespective of its objective function. The objective function cannot decorrelate what sits upstream of it. The document never names this residual, never bounds it, and never qualifies rule 6's instruction to treat convergence as wanted signal by 'after the shared-blind-spot residual is bounded'. The defensible version of decorrelation is 'opposed objectives reduce, but do not eliminate, correlation; the irreducible floor is the shared model + shared rubric'; the manuscript instead reads as if opposed objectives deliver near-independence.
why_it_matters: This is the strongest argument my rival (S09) will press, and the honest defender must concede its core: convergence among heads that share an unmodeled blind spot is not independent corroboration. Because rule 6 explicitly forbids down-weighting convergence and the synthesizer uses raised_by_n_blind_seats as a salience signal, an unbounded shared-blind-spot correlation could let a base-model-wide false positive be amplified by agreement and 'laundered' — precisely the failure mode SKILL.md s47 says the rails exist to prevent. Leaving the residual unstated means the tool cannot tell the author how much weight agreement actually deserves.
proposed_fix: Add one paragraph (in shared_grounding_rules rule 6 or DESIGN §2.2) acknowledging the irreducible shared-substrate floor: opposed objective functions decorrelate the search, not the shared weights/rubric/quote-gate; therefore convergence is signal *conditional on* the inter-seat overlap diagnostic showing the heads disagreed elsewhere, and a flaw class the base model is blind to will be missed by all seats alike. Tie the existing external-dissent leg (rule 9) explicitly to this gap as the partial mitigation it already is.
risk_of_fix: Stating the floor too starkly could be quoted out of context as 'the authors admit their fleet is correlated' and undercut adoption; phrase it as the standard, expected limit of any single-model ensemble (which every honest multi-agent system shares), not as a defect unique to this tool.

location.section: README.md (public claims) s152-s153 vs s153 / DESIGN v1 §2.2 s537

quote:
Every contested methodological choice is staffed by ≥2
  seats from **rival schools**, instantiated with *opposed objective functions*
issue: Two of my owned claims sit one sentence apart and are in apparent tension. C-020 ('staffed by ≥2 seats from rival schools') and the README's 'competing/rival traditions' framing locate the decorrelation in DISCIPLINARY identity (schools, traditions) — exactly what the very next sentence, C-021 ('Real disagreement, not disciplinary costume'), and DESIGN §2.2 ('Decorrelation comes from rival objective functions in separate heads, not job titles') disavow as costume. A generous reading reconciles them — the 'school/tradition' fixes the topic JURISDICTION a seat covers, while the OPPOSED OBJECTIVE FUNCTION is the actual decorrelator — and that reconciliation is coherent. But the manuscript never states it; the two mechanisms are named as co-equal ('rival schools, instantiated with opposed objective functions') without saying which one is load-bearing, so a reader is left with a claim that simultaneously relies on and repudiates disciplinary framing.
why_it_matters: The seat architecture is the product's signature. If the public README cannot keep straight whether disagreement comes from schools or from objective functions, a referee reasonably concludes the team has not decided which mechanism it is actually selling — and the 'not disciplinary costume' tagline looks contradicted by the design that staffs 'rival schools'. The defensible reading is one sentence away; making it explicit removes an apparent self-contradiction at zero cost to the mechanism.
proposed_fix: State the division of labor once, where the seats are introduced: 'Disciplinary tradition fixes WHAT a seat is expert in; the opposed objective function fixes the DIRECTION it argues — the latter is the decorrelator, the former just ensures topic coverage. School without opposed objective is costume; objective function is the mechanism.' Then C-020 and C-021 are complementary, not contradictory.
risk_of_fix: Minimal. Over-elaborating could turn a crisp README bullet into a methods lecture; one clause suffices.

location.section: shared_grounding_rules.md rule 6 (s337-s338) / DESIGN v1 §4 item 9 (s602)

issue: The 'inter-seat overlap diagnostic' is named three times (rule 6: overlap 'reported as a diagnostic the author weighs'; DESIGN item 9: 'report an inter-seat overlap diagnostic (never an auto-down-weighter)') as the instrument that makes convergence interpretable, but it is never operationalized: the document does not define what 'overlap' is measured over (finding text? located span? claim-id? severity?), what threshold distinguishes 'genuine convergence' from 'redundant restatement', or how the author is supposed to 'weigh' it. For a defender this matters acutely — the diagnostic is the ONLY proposed evidence that the heads decorrelated at all, yet it has no stated metric. An undefined diagnostic cannot discharge the burden that C-021/C-034 place on it.
why_it_matters: Rule 6 forbids auto-down-weighting convergence and instead hands the author a diagnostic to judge it; if that diagnostic is undefined, the author is given a label, not a measurement, and cannot actually tell decorrelated agreement from correlated echo. This is the missing load-bearing instrument behind the entire 'convergence is signal' stance — without an operational definition, the decorrelation claim has no observable that could confirm or falsify it.
proposed_fix: Specify the diagnostic concretely: e.g. report, per finding cluster, how many blind seats raised it AND their objective-function mix (did both a 'fatal-flaw' and a 'defensible-version' seat independently land on it?), plus a pairwise overlap rate over located spans across the fleet as a whole. Define what counts as agreement (same claim-id or overlapping sentence range, not merely similar prose) and state how a high vs low fleet-wide overlap should change the author's read.
risk_of_fix: A poorly chosen overlap metric could itself mislead (e.g. counting near-duplicate prose as agreement inflates apparent convergence). Pilot the metric on the planned ablation before publishing it as the headline diagnostic.

tradition: Generalist (relevance / so-what) — distinguished outsider, not a multi-agent-systems specialist

location.section: Whole document; superlatives concentrated in SKILL.md (entry point & claims), README.md (public claims), and DESIGN v1 §2.4; the evidence is deferred in DESIGN v1 §6 item 8

quote: use it to *tune the default fan-out* and headline the README with a real number — not as a gate.
issue: Read from the outside, this is a document that sells a finished, trustworthy, superlative product while admitting — in one buried clause — that the evidence for it does not yet exist. The whole text is architecture and zero outcome: it promises 'the best feedback achievable', a result 'better than any conference', an 'impeccable revised paper', and a fleet you 'can trust', yet it never shows a single review the tool produced, a single paper it improved, or a single recall / false-positive number. The one thing that could substantiate any of the marketing — the 4-arm ablation that would 'headline the README with a real number' — is parked in a 'parallel, non-blocking' validation track and 'not [used] as a gate'. So by the author's own design, the product can ship and be called 'better than any conference' before anyone has measured whether it catches real flaws or manufactures false ones. Even if every mechanism in here works exactly as written, the document never establishes that the output is good; it asserts that it is.
why_it_matters: Relevance is the question of whether the contribution matters, and a tool's contribution is its output, not its org chart. A reader cannot tell from this document whether the thing is worth running, because the only claims that bear on output quality are unmeasured superlatives. For a methodology that brands itself on 'Ground, don't recall; never fabricate', headlining its own description with unvalidated 'better than any conference' / 'impeccable' claims is the same sin one level up. This is desk-reject-grade for an empirical or methods venue: the central value proposition is asserted, not demonstrated, and the document does not concede that it is unestablished where it makes the boast.
proposed_fix: Demote every outcome superlative ('better than any conference', 'the best feedback achievable', 'impeccable', 'you can trust a 300-agent run') to a clearly-labelled design aspiration until the ablation exists, OR make the validation track a release gate and report at least one real recall/false-positive result before any such phrasing is used. At minimum, add an explicit, prominent caveat at the point of each boast: 'Unvalidated as of this version; the recall/FP study (§6.8) has not been run.'
risk_of_fix: Softening the marketing language could make the tool sound weaker than a future validated version actually is; the fix must be reversible once real numbers exist, and must not be read as conceding the architecture is unsound (it is the evidence, not the design, that is missing).

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) §3.1 and prompts/shared_grounding_rules.md item 13; the reader-facing payoff is in README.md (public claims) 'Why you can trust a 300-agent run'

quote: This makes fabrication structurally impossible — the data/code analogue of Act I's quote+locator rule.
issue: The headline reason a busy reader is told to care — that you 'can trust a 300-agent run' because 'fabrication [is] structurally impossible' and 'invented numbers are structurally impossible' — is a stronger promise than the described machinery can keep, and an outsider spots the gap immediately. The Wall guarantees that every number CARRIES a provenance token tracing to a logged run; it does not guarantee the number is the RIGHT one for the sentence it lands in. A Scribe that 'only transcribes a value carrying a provenance token' can still transcribe the wrong tagged value, attach it to the wrong claim, or pull a token from a run of buggy author code — none of which the provenance check detects. 'Structurally impossible' describes invented-from-nothing fabrication; it is oversold as a blanket trust guarantee for the output. The same overreach recurs in the Act-I quote-gate (a verbatim substring match proves a quote exists, not that the criticism built on it is correct).
why_it_matters: The single most important thing this document is trying to make me believe — that scale does not buy confident nonsense — rests on the word 'structurally impossible'. If that word is doing more work than the mechanism supports, the contribution's importance is overstated at exactly the load-bearing point. A neighbouring-field reader who takes 'structurally impossible' at face value will trust an output that can still be wrong in precisely the ways that matter (wrong number on the right-looking provenance tag). Calibrating this claim is the difference between a genuinely trustworthy tool and one that has merely relocated where the trust must be placed.
proposed_fix: Replace 'structurally impossible' with what the mechanism actually delivers: 'every number is forced to carry a re-run provenance token, so a number invented from nothing cannot enter — but the tool still relies on the Scribe attaching the right value to the right claim and on the author's code being correct.' Frame the Wall and the quote-gate as necessary, not sufficient, conditions for trust, and state the residual failure modes they do not close.
risk_of_fix: Stating residual failure modes could be read by a skimming user as 'the tool fabricates numbers', which is the opposite of true; the rewrite must be precise that invented-from-nothing numbers are blocked while wrong-but-provenanced numbers are the remaining (smaller) risk.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims) §2.2 / depth-tier table and SKILL.md (entry point & claims); cost framing in 'Runtime is not a constraint'

quote: Runtime is not a constraint — a monumental run takes hours by design.
issue: Nowhere does the document argue that the marginal value of this machine justifies its marginal cost. It proposes runs of '~300–600' agent instantiations taking 'hours by design', and positions itself as an extension of the cheaper, faster mad-research — yet it never answers the obvious outsider question: what does a 300-agent, multi-hour run catch that a 15-agent 'quick' run, or a single careful human read, or the existing mad-research memo, does not? 'Runtime is not a constraint' is stated as a virtue, but for any real user runtime, token cost, and attention are constraints, and the document offers no evidence that the exhaustive tier finds materially more true flaws (rather than more marginal false positives) than a small one. The contribution may be real, but its IMPORTANCE relative to the alternatives — including its own cheaper tiers — is simply assumed.
why_it_matters: A tool can be rigorous and still not worth its cost; that is precisely the relevance question a generalist is seated to ask. If the monumental tier does not demonstrably beat the quick tier or the prior-art memo on true-flaw recall, then the headline contribution ('the largest possible Claude-only expert fleet') is engineering for its own sake, and the right product is the cheap version. location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims)

quote: This makes fabrication structurally impossible — the data/code analogue of Act I's quote+locator rule.

location.section: SKILL.md (entry point & claims); examples/ (self-audit)

issue: The document under review is the tool's own design document, and the worked 'example' is the tool reviewing itself (the self-audit). Nowhere does the document acknowledge that self-application provides no independent evidence for its central 'it works / it's better' claim. For any empirical field, a method whose only demonstration is being run on itself is the textbook circularity problem: the artifact and its evaluator share every bias, blind spot, and failure mode, so a clean self-audit is consistent with the tool being excellent and equally consistent with it being uniformly blind in the same place the design is. To a neighboring discipline assessing whether this contribution is credible enough to matter, the absence of any external, independent test — and the absence of even a sentence conceding that self-review cannot establish effectiveness — is a significant silence. The cross-field reader's first question, 'would this catch a flaw the authors themselves would miss?', is structurally unanswerable from a self-audit and is never addressed.
why_it_matters: Significance claims must be backed by evidence that does not presuppose the conclusion. Validating a reviewer by having it review its own design doc cannot speak to whether it would help a real, independent author — the only thing that would make it matter to the wider field. Leaving this unstated lets a reader over-credit the self-audit as evidence of quality when it is evidence of nothing of the sort.
proposed_fix: State explicitly that the self-audit is a development exercise, not evidence of effectiveness, and that the central effectiveness claim requires independent application to papers the tool did not author (the planned ablation on real, third-party papers with planted flaws and certified-clean passages). Until that exists, scope the significance claims to 'designed to' rather than 'does'.
risk_of_fix: Admitting the self-audit proves nothing about effectiveness removes the only concrete demonstration currently on offer and exposes how much of the significance case is still aspirational; the document must avoid over-correcting into self-deprecation that obscures the design's real merits.

location.section: DESIGN v1 (full architecture & claims)

issue: The design promises an 'importance/relevance memo from the generalists' as a deliverable, i.e. the tool will pronounce on whether a reviewed paper matters and whether its claims travel. location.section: SKILL.md depth-tier table / Design v1 §6.8 'Validation track'

location.section: Design v1 §3.1 / shared_grounding_rules.md rule 13 / §4.1

quote: Implement via separate roles: a **Runner** (executes code, cannot edit prose) and a **Scribe** (edits prose, cannot invent numbers — only transcribes a provenance-tagged value).
issue: The document repeatedly asserts that the Runner/Scribe split makes fabrication 'structurally impossible' and 'Invented numbers are structurally impossible,' but the separation is enforced only by instructions to two prompts of the same model — there is no type system, OS boundary, or external referee that physically prevents a 'Scribe' context from emitting a number that no provenance token backs. 'Cannot' here means 'is told not to,' which is exactly the kind of claim a single counterexample falsifies. A reviewer who has watched an LLM ignore a system instruction once will treat 'structurally impossible' as a red flag that the authors overstate their own guarantees, and the moment anyone exhibits one un-provenanced number that slipped through (trivially producible in adversarial testing), the paper's flagship integrity claim is publicly broken.

proposed_fix: Replace every 'structurally impossible' / 'cannot' with the accurate mechanism-level claim: the Scribe is *instructed* to transcribe only provenance-tagged values and a *deterministic* post-hoc Consistency Reconciler rejects any number lacking a token. risk_of_fix: Honest wording is less impressive and removes a marquee selling point. The alternative — leaving a falsifiable absolute claim in a tool that touches the scientific record — is the larger risk.

tradition: Statistical-independence / ensemble-methods school (N draws from one model are not N independent experts; correlated error is invisible to the correlated checker)

location.section: shared_grounding_rules.md rule 5–6 / Design v1 §2.1.D

quote: Specialist seats review in isolation and **lock** their findings before seeing any peer. This is the only thing that makes a same-model fleet more than N correlated draws.
issue: The document stakes the whole 'monumental fleet' value proposition on the premise that commit-and-reveal plus 'opposed objective functions' converts correlated same-model draws into genuine independence — and it provides no evidence this overcomes shared-model blind spots, while elsewhere conceding the exact failure mode that defeats it: 'An LLM verifier shares the hallucination it is checking.' If that is true for the quote angle (the reason the quote-gate must be a script), it is equally true for the logic, severity, decision-relevance, steelman, and factual-literature angles, which are ALL run by the same model family. A blind spot common to the base model is invisible to 600 copies of it and to every LLM verifier downstream, no matter the role labels; scaling the fleet then buys correlated false confidence, not coverage. This is the failure mode that produces the catastrophic version of this tool: a confident 'monumental' green light on a paper with a flaw the model class systematically cannot see.
why_it_matters: The README headline is literally 'Why you can trust a 300-agent run'; if the only mechanism distinguishing the fleet from N correlated draws is asserted rather than demonstrated, and the document itself supplies the principle (shared hallucination) that breaks it for all non-script angles, then the central justification for scale is unsupported — and 'more agents' may *increase* the risk of laundering a fatal flaw into a confident green light, the precise outcome the rails claim to prevent.
proposed_fix: State the residual-correlation limitation explicitly and prominently: same-model seats reduce some independent-error variance but cannot detect errors common to the base model; therefore the cross-model external dissent leg should be a default non-optional component (not 'skipped + disclosed'), and the validation track must report whether added agents actually raise recall or only raise agreement. Stop claiming scale yields independence; claim only that it yields breadth of attention, and back even that with the deferred measurement.
risk_of_fix: Acknowledging irreducible correlation undercuts the 'largest possible Claude fleet' marketing and the 'Claude-only' positioning. The risk of NOT acknowledging it is a public failure where a scaled run confidently misses a model-class blind spot.

tradition: Verification-theory school (a checker that shares the generator's failure modes provides no independent assurance; only the deterministic gates are real)

location.section: helpers/verification_panel.md / shared_grounding_rules.md rule 8 & rule 10

quote: An LLM verifier shares the hallucination it is checking, so this gate is a **script**, fail-closed.
issue: The document grounds its single strongest safeguard (the quote-gate) on the admission that LLM verifiers share the generator's hallucinations — yet it then sells a seven-angle 'multi-angle independent verification before delivery' panel in which six of the seven angles (logical-validity, factual-literature, severity-calibration, decision-relevance, steelman-charity, fix-safety) are run by that same hallucination-sharing LLM, and only the quote-locator angle is a script. By the document's own stated principle, those six angles cannot be trusted to catch errors the base model is disposed to make; stacking '2 independent verifiers per angle (majority within an angle)' multiplies correlated judgments, not independent ones. So the marquee phrase 'Nothing reaches the author until several independent subagents... have checked it' overstates the assurance: for everything except verbatim quote existence, the 'check' is the same mind grading its own work. The embarrassing future is a delivered High finding that is logically invalid or factually wrong, cleared by a 'verified' panel, because the invalidity was a shared model blind spot.
why_it_matters: This contradiction sits at the load-bearing center of the trust story (rule 8 is the feature 'that lets the tool be monumental without being a confident-nonsense generator'). If the document concedes LLM verifiers share hallucinations but still markets LLM verification as independent assurance, the rails are weaker than advertised exactly where the stakes are highest, and the 'verified' label on a finding becomes misleading.
proposed_fix: Distinguish, in verification_panel.md and the README, the deterministic gates (quote_gate.py, numeric-provenance hashing, the Consistency Reconciler) — which are genuinely independent of the model — from the LLM angles, which are NOT, and label the latter as 'reduces but does not eliminate correlated error.' Reserve the word 'verified' for the script-backed angles; call the LLM-angle outcome 'reviewed by independent prompts' and require at least one genuinely out-of-model (cross-provider) check before any High finding is asserted as fact rather than 'needs-author-confirmation.'
risk_of_fix: Downgrading 'verified' to 'reviewed' for most angles deflates the central marketing claim and forces a dependency on a non-Claude leg the design wants to keep optional. The countervailing risk — a 'verified' but wrong finding shipped to an author who trusted the label — is worse.

tradition: Measurement-validity school (coverage of attention is not coverage of correctness; a completeness proof that proves the former while being marketed as the latter is a category error)

location.section: Design v1 §2.3 & §2.4 / README 'Exhaustive to the sentence'

quote: the paper is tiled into disjoint sentence ranges and a completeness audit certifies `covered == total` — "every argument, every word" is a *checked invariant*, not a slogan.
issue: The 'completeness certificate' proves only that some seat *returned a verdict for* every sentence range — it cannot and does not certify that every error was found, yet the document markets it as 'a printed guarantee every claim and sentence was examined' and the reason the tool 'beats any conference.' This is coverage theater: `covered == total` is satisfied by a seat glancing at a range and finding nothing, so a fatal flaw sitting inside a 'covered' sentence yields a 100%-coverage certificate that is simultaneously wrong. The catastrophic future writes itself: the tool issues a completeness certificate, the author submits trusting 'every word was examined,' a referee finds an elementary error in a sentence the certificate marked covered, and the headline guarantee becomes the object of ridicule — the certificate's existence makes the miss look like negligence rather than oversight.
why_it_matters: The completeness certificate is sold as a differentiator and a trust anchor ('a printed guarantee'); conflating attention-coverage with correctness-coverage sets a false expectation that a single counterexample (inevitable, since no reviewer is complete) converts into a credibility collapse. Honest scoping here is the difference between a useful coverage ledger and an overpromise that invites humiliation.
proposed_fix: Rename and rescope the certificate to exactly what it proves: 'every sentence range received reviewer attention and a recorded verdict' — explicitly NOT a guarantee of correctness or that all errors were found. Strike 'guarantee every claim and sentence was examined' framing that implies exhaustive error-detection, and add a standing caveat that completeness of attention does not imply completeness of findings.
risk_of_fix: The honest version is less marketable than 'every argument, every word, guaranteed.' But the inflated version is a falsifiable promise that one missed error destroys, so the deflation is protective.

tradition: Reproducibility / claims-must-be-demonstrated school (a 'genuinely runnable, clean-room-replicated' package asserted with zero worked examples is a falsifiable promise)

location.section: README Act II / SKILL.md Files block / Design v1 §3.6 & §7

quote: Assembles a genuinely runnable **replication package** (AEA/TOP-compatible) whose `MAP.md` ties every table, figure, and headline number to the exact script that produced it — and clean-room-replicates it to prove it reproduces.
issue: The README promises that Act II clean-room-replicates the package 'to prove it reproduces,' and the SKILL.md Files block lists an `examples/` directory of `self-audit/`, while the Design v1 §7 names pilots in the future tense ('Exercises BOTH phases,' 'forces... to auto-instantiate (first Scout correctness check)') — i.e., Act II has apparently never been run end-to-end on real data/code, yet the strongest operational claim (a reproducing replication package) is stated as a present capability. The moment one user points Act II at a real `.do`/`.R`/`.py` project and the master script does not reproduce the embedded numbers — overwhelmingly likely on first contact with real-world code, environments, and seeds — the 'genuinely runnable' / 'clean-room-replicates... to prove it reproduces' claim is publicly falsified, and because Act II edits toward the scientific record, the failure is not cosmetic: it is a tool that promised reproduction and instead handed back a non-reproducing artifact under a trust label.
why_it_matters: Act II is explicitly named 'the moat — nothing in the lineage does it'; the entire competitive claim rests on a capability with no demonstrated successful run in the manuscript. An unrun moat is a liability, not a differentiator: it is the single most likely place for an early, public, embarrassing failure.
proposed_fix: Do not claim Act II 'clean-room-replicates... to prove it reproduces' as a present capability until at least one full pilot (the named `optimal_inflation/` target) has been run end-to-end and the worked example is shipped in `examples/`. Until then, label Act II as 'planned/under validation,' and ensure the README's reproduction promise is gated on the baseline-reproduction result actually succeeding, with the honest-labeling rule (rule 15) applied loudly when it does not.
risk_of_fix: Demoting the moat to 'planned' undercuts the core differentiation versus mad-research. But shipping it as proven without a worked example is the higher-variance failure, since reproduction failures are near-certain on first real contact.

tradition: Independence / conflict-of-interest school (a system grading its own design, synthesized by copies of itself, with the only external check optional, is not an audit)

location.section: Design v1 header note / SKILL.md Safety defaults / précis framing

quote: *Synthesized 2026-06-05 from 4 parallel design subagents (Phase-1 fleet, Phase-2 implementation, integrity rails, naming+roadmap).
issue: The manuscript under review is the tool's own design document, the document was itself produced by the same Claude-subagent architecture it describes, and the self-audit is being run by that architecture on itself — while the ONLY out-of-model check (the 'external dissent leg') is, by the document's own rule, optional and 'skipped + disclosed if no compliant endpoint,' and the document states flatly there is 'no Bayesian mode; there is no exception' and the tool is 'Claude-only.' That is a closed epistemic loop: the same model class designs the tool, writes its claims, audits the claims, and verifies the audit, with no mandatory independent eye anywhere. A skeptical reviewer (or a journalist) will frame the eventual self-published 'we audited ourselves and passed' as exactly the conflict of interest peer review exists to prevent, and any later external failure becomes a story about a self-certifying system that marked its own homework — the most reputationally damaging way for an integrity-branded tool to fail.
why_it_matters: The tool's entire pitch is integrity-at-scale; if its own flagship self-audit lacks a single mandatory independent check, the credibility of every 'verified' / 'certified' label is undermined by association. Independence is not a feature to make optional in the one demonstration that is supposed to prove the tool's trustworthiness.
proposed_fix: For any self-audit or first-party validation, make at least one genuinely independent check mandatory and non-skippable (cross-provider dissent and/or a named human reviewer), and disclose in the self-audit report that a single-model system cannot validate itself. Reframe the self-audit as 'a design pass, pending independent and human review,' not as evidence of trustworthiness.
risk_of_fix: Requiring an external/human leg breaks the 'Claude-only' purity and adds dependency and cost. The alternative — a self-certifying integrity tool — is the worse position to defend publicly.
